subject: Paediatrics
q: A preterm neonate born at 30 weeks develops abdominal distension, bilious aspirates, and blood-streaked stools on day 10 of life. Abdominal X-ray shows pneumatosis intestinalis. Which subsequent radiographic finding would be an absolute indication for emergency laparotomy?
opts: A single fixed dilated bowel loop on serial films
why: Diagnostic of NEC but not by itself an absolute surgical indication; managed medically first
A fixed dilated loop suggests impending perforation/necrosis but is a relative, not absolute, indication
Portal venous gas indicates severe disease and is a poor prognostic sign but is also a relative indication in most protocols
Correct - pneumoperitoneum signifies bowel perforation, the one universally agreed absolute surgical indication
exp: In necrotizing enterocolitis, medical management (bowel rest, IV antibiotics, TPN) is first-line; pneumoperitoneum on X-ray, signifying perforation, is the only universally agreed absolute indication for surgery, while a fixed loop, portal venous gas, or clinical deterioration despite medical therapy are relative indications weighed together. The exact relative-indication list can vary slightly by protocol.

subject: Paediatrics
q: A term infant born small for gestational age (birth weight 2.1 kg, less than 3rd centile) continues to track below the 3rd centile for both weight and height at 4 years of age despite adequate nutritional intake. What is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Reassure the family that catch-up growth will still occur later in childhood
Start only a high-calorie supplemental diet and reassess in a year
Evaluate the child for growth hormone therapy
Repeat anthropometric measurements after 6 months before any action
why: Most SGA infants show catch-up growth well before 4 years; failure by then should not simply be reassured away
Dietary optimization alone is insufficient once failure to catch up by IAP's 4-year criterion is established
Correct - per IAP's approach to short stature, SGA infants who fail to catch up by 4 years are candidates for growth hormone therapy evaluation, distinct from classic GH deficiency
Further watchful waiting delays a time-sensitive intervention once the 4-year criterion is met
exp: Per IAP's approach to short stature, SGA infants who fail to show catch-up growth by 4 years of age are a distinct, recognized indication for growth hormone therapy evaluation, separate from classic GH deficiency - this is the age point IAP practice uses to move from watchful waiting to work-up.

subject: Paediatrics
q: A 3-month-old infant, born after a pregnancy complicated by maternal polyhydramnios, presents with failure to thrive and polyuria. Investigations reveal hypokalemia, metabolic alkalosis, and normal blood pressure. Which diagnosis best fits this picture?
why: Gitelman syndrome typically presents later with hypomagnesemia and hypocalciuria, without antenatal polyhydramnios
Correct - antenatal Bartter syndrome presents with polyhydramnios, postnatal salt-wasting, hypokalemic alkalosis, and normal blood pressure
Liddle syndrome causes hypertension with hypokalemic alkalosis via ENaC overactivity, not salt-wasting
Distal RTA causes hypokalemic metabolic acidosis, not alkalosis
exp: Bartter syndrome results from a defect mimicking loop diuretic action in the thick ascending limb, producing antenatal polyhydramnios, salt-wasting, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis, and normotension - the polyhydramnios and early infantile onset are the key discriminators from the later-presenting, hypomagnesemic Gitelman syndrome.

subject: Paediatrics
q: A 12-year-old obese boy presents with a limp and referred pain in the knee for 3 weeks. On examination, the hip shows restricted internal rotation with obligatory external rotation of the hip on passive flexion. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why: Correct - SCFE classically occurs in obese adolescents with knee-referred pain and the pathognomonic obligatory external rotation on hip flexion (Drehmann sign)
Perthes disease occurs at 4-8 years, typically lean active boys, without the obligatory external rotation sign
Septic arthritis presents acutely with fever and inability to bear weight, not a 3-week indolent course
Transient synovitis is acute, self-limited, and follows a viral illness, without this exam finding
exp: SCFE is a Salter-Harris type I fracture through the proximal femoral physis, classically in an obese adolescent; the Drehmann sign (obligatory external rotation on passive hip flexion) is a key bedside discriminator from Perthes disease and septic arthritis.

subject: Paediatrics
q: A 10-month-old infant had high-grade fever for 3 days with no localizing symptoms and looked relatively well between fever spikes. The fever resolved abruptly, followed by the appearance of a rose-pink maculopapular rash over the trunk that spread to the limbs. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why: Rubella causes mild fever with the rash appearing concurrently, plus post-auricular lymphadenopathy, not this fever-then-rash sequence
Measles shows the rash appearing while fever is still high, with preceding coryza, conjunctivitis, and Koplik spots
Scarlet fever shows a sandpaper rash with strawberry tongue concurrent with fever, following streptococcal pharyngitis
Correct - roseola infantum is defined by fever for 3-4 days in a well-appearing infant, followed by abrupt defervescence then rash
exp: Roseola infantum (exanthem subitum, sixth disease), caused by HHV-6, is distinctive for its sequence: rash appears only after the fever breaks, in an otherwise well-looking infant typically aged 6 months to 2 years; febrile seizures are a recognized complication during the febrile phase.

subject: Paediatrics
q: A 6-month-old infant with recurrent chest infections and poor weight gain despite a good appetite is noted to pass greasy, foul-smelling, bulky stools. A sweat chloride test performed on two separate occasions shows values of 68 and 72 mEq/L. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why: Primary ciliary dyskinesia causes recurrent sinopulmonary infections but a normal sweat chloride test
Celiac disease causes malabsorptive steatorrhea and failure to thrive but not recurrent chest infections or elevated sweat chloride
Correct - a sweat chloride greater than 60 mEq/L on two occasions with respiratory and pancreatic-insufficiency features is diagnostic of cystic fibrosis
Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency causes early emphysema and neonatal cholestasis, not this triad, and does not elevate sweat chloride
exp: Cystic fibrosis (CFTR gene defect) produces thick secretions causing recurrent pulmonary infections, exocrine pancreatic insufficiency (steatorrhea, failure to thrive), and elevated sweat chloride (greater than 60 mEq/L, confirmed on repeat testing) - the sweat chloride test remains the diagnostic gold standard alongside genetic testing and newborn screening.

subject: Paediatrics
q: A 6-day-old term neonate who has been exclusively fed whole (unmodified) cow's milk presents with jitteriness followed by a generalized seizure. Investigations show low serum calcium with elevated serum phosphate and normal magnesium. What is the most likely mechanism for these findings?
opts: Early neonatal hypocalcemia related to prematurity
Late neonatal hypocalcemia due to a high phosphate load from whole cow's milk
why: Early neonatal hypocalcemia typically occurs within the first 72 hours in preterm, IDM, or asphyxiated infants, not day 6 in a term infant
Correct - late neonatal hypocalcemia classically follows feeding with high-phosphate whole cow's milk, overwhelming the immature neonatal kidney's phosphate excretion
DiGeorge syndrome would present with hypocalcemia from birth plus other features, not this feeding-related pattern with normal magnesium
Vitamin D deficiency rickets presents later in infancy with low calcium and phosphate together with elevated alkaline phosphatase, not this acute pattern
exp: Late neonatal hypocalcemia is classically precipitated by feeding whole, unmodified cow's milk, because it has much higher phosphate content than breast milk and the immature neonatal kidney cannot excrete the excess load, causing reciprocal hypocalcemia - standard infant formula is phosphate-adjusted and does not cause this, so exclusive breastfeeding or appropriate formula counseling is the reinforcement point.

subject: Paediatrics
q: During inpatient nutritional rehabilitation for a child with severe acute malnutrition and bilateral pedal edema, high-calorie feeds started on day 3 trigger sudden weakness, respiratory distress, and a new cardiac arrhythmia, with serum phosphate returning low. Which complication is this?
why: Occurs early/before feeding, not after high-calorie feeds are started.
Correct -- rapid calorie reintroduction causes an insulin surge driving phosphate intracellularly.
Causes ophthalmoplegia/ataxia/confusion from thiamine deficiency, not phosphate-driven arrhythmia.
Causes raised intracranial pressure and skin changes, not this picture.
exp: Refeeding syndrome follows rapid reintroduction of calories in a malnourished child: an insulin surge drives phosphate (and potassium, magnesium) intracellularly, and resulting hypophosphatemia impairs ATP synthesis, causing arrhythmia and respiratory weakness -- why SAM protocols start with cautious low-calorie F-75 feeds.

subject: Paediatrics
q: A 9-year-old boy has severe epigastric pain radiating to the back, repeated vomiting, and abdominal tenderness. Serum lipase is 4 times the upper limit of normal. Image described: ultrasound shows a bulky, hypoechoic pancreas. How many of the three diagnostic criteria (pain, enzyme rise, imaging) does this child meet, and what is the diagnosis?
opts: All three criteria met -- acute pancreatitis
Only two criteria met -- pancreatitis excluded
Enzyme rise alone is diagnostic regardless of pain or imaging
Imaging alone is diagnostic; enzymes are not required
why: Correct -- pain, enzyme rise over 3x ULN, and imaging are all present.
Two criteria alone are sufficient, and this case meets all three anyway.
Enzyme rise alone without pain or imaging is not diagnostic.
Imaging alone without supportive enzymes or pain is not diagnostic.
exp: Acute pancreatitis diagnosis needs 2 of 3: characteristic pain, lipase/amylase over 3x ULN, and confirmatory imaging (revised Atlanta criteria, applied similarly in children); paediatric causes include idiopathic, biliary, drug-induced, and mumps/viral aetiologies.

subject: Paediatrics
q: An 8-month-old girl's weight tracked along the 50th percentile at 4 months but has now dropped below the 15th percentile, crossing two major percentile channels on the WHO growth chart. Other parameters appear proportionate. What does this pattern define?
opts: Normal growth variation, no action needed
why: Crossing two major channels is never a normal variant.
A pubertal/linear-growth pattern in older children with family history, not an infant weight-crossing pattern.
Correct -- defined by a fall across two or more major percentile lines over time.
Catch-up growth is percentile-gaining, the opposite pattern.
exp: Growth faltering (failure to thrive) is defined by a fall across two or more major percentile lines on a growth chart over time, regardless of the absolute percentile reached, and warrants systematic evaluation for organic and non-organic causes.

subject: Paediatrics
q: A term neonate, well for the first 48 hours, develops poor feeding and lethargy progressing to seizures on day 3. Arterial blood gas shows respiratory alkalosis (not metabolic acidosis), plasma ammonia is markedly elevated, and the anion gap is normal. Which category of inborn error of metabolism best fits this picture?
why: Typically shows metabolic acidosis with an elevated anion gap.
Presents with jaundice, hepatomegaly, cataracts, and E. coli sepsis risk, not this ammonia/gas pattern.
Presents with hypoketotic hypoglycemia, not primarily respiratory alkalosis.
Correct -- hyperammonemia drives respiratory alkalosis without metabolic acidosis.
exp: Urea cycle disorders present with hyperammonemia that drives central hyperventilation and respiratory alkalosis, classically without metabolic acidosis or anion gap -- a key bedside discriminator from organic acidemias, which pair hyperammonemia with a high anion-gap metabolic acidosis.

subject: Paediatrics
q: A term neonate develops central cyanosis at 6 hours of life, unresponsive to 100% oxygen. Image described: pulse oximetry shows SpO2 96% on the right hand (pre-ductal) versus 82% on the left foot (post-ductal), a difference exceeding 10%. What does this finding most strongly suggest?
opts: Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn (PPHN)
why: Causes tachypnoea from retained fetal lung fluid, without this saturation gradient or oxygen-refractory cyanosis.
Correct -- a pre/post-ductal SpO2 gradient over 5-10% indicates right-to-left shunting from elevated pulmonary vascular resistance.
Also causes oxygen-refractory cyanosis, but from parallel circulations -- pre- and post-ductal saturations are typically similar, not split by more than 10%.
Causes cyclical cyanosis relieved by crying (mouth-breathing), not a fixed pre/post-ductal gradient.
exp: A pre-ductal to post-ductal SpO2 gradient greater than 5-10% indicates right-to-left shunting across a patent ductus arteriosus due to elevated pulmonary vascular resistance -- the hallmark bedside clue to PPHN, confirmed by echocardiography and a failed hyperoxia test.

subject: Paediatrics
q: A 14-year-old boy has fever, severe exudative pharyngitis, tender cervical lymphadenopathy, and splenomegaly. Started empirically on amoxicillin for presumed streptococcal pharyngitis, he develops a diffuse, itchy maculopapular rash over trunk and limbs on day 3. What is the most likely diagnosis, and what does the rash represent?
opts: Infectious mononucleosis (EBV); a non-allergic drug-triggered rash, not true penicillin allergy
Streptococcal pharyngitis with scarlet fever rash
why: Correct -- EBV mono classically causes an amoxicillin-triggered maculopapular rash, a non-IgE-mediated reaction.
Scarlet fever's sandpaper rash is toxin-mediated and needs no drug trigger.
Measles has a cephalocaudal rash with Koplik spots and coryza, a distinct picture.
SJS is a severe mucocutaneous blistering reaction, not a diffuse maculopapular rash.
exp: EBV infectious mononucleosis classically causes an amoxicillin/ampicillin-induced maculopapular rash in a large majority of affected patients -- a non-IgE-mediated reaction rather than true penicillin allergy; exudative pharyngitis with lymphadenopathy and splenomegaly should prompt EBV serology before empirical amoxicillin.

subject: Paediatrics
q: A 5-year-old boy with nephrotic syndrome shows no remission of proteinuria despite 4 weeks of daily prednisolone at standard dose (2 mg/kg/day). What is the next appropriate step and the most likely underlying histology?
opts: Renal biopsy - most likely focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS)
Continue the same steroid course for another 8 weeks without biopsy
Start ACE inhibitors alone and observe
Renal biopsy - most likely minimal change disease
why: Correct - steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome mandates biopsy, and FSGS is the most common histology found.
Prolonging the same regimen without escalation/biopsy risks ongoing renal injury and delays diagnosis.
A useful antiproteinuric adjunct but does not substitute for establishing a histological diagnosis in steroid resistance.
Minimal change disease is the typical finding in steroid-responsive, not steroid-resistant, nephrotic syndrome.
exp: Failure to achieve remission after 4 weeks of daily prednisolone at standard dose defines steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome, which mandates a renal biopsy before escalating immunosuppression; FSGS is the most common histology in steroid-resistant cases, in contrast to minimal change disease, which dominates the steroid-responsive group.

subject: Paediatrics
q: A term, appropriate-for-gestational-age neonate at 6 hours of life is jittery and lethargic; blood glucose is 38 mg/dL. What is the most appropriate immediate management?
opts: Recheck glucose in 6 hours with no intervention if the baby appears well
Treat as symptomatic hypoglycemia - IV dextrose bolus followed by infusion, since the level is below the treatment threshold for a symptomatic infant
Start oral formula only and recheck in 24 hours
No action is needed, as this is a normal newborn glucose value
why: Delaying treatment in a symptomatic infant risks ongoing neuroglycopenia.
Correct - a symptomatic neonate below the treatment threshold needs prompt IV dextrose, not observation.
Oral feeding alone may be tried first only in an asymptomatic at-risk infant with borderline levels, not a symptomatic one.
38 mg/dL with symptoms is not a reassuring/normal value requiring no action.
exp: For a symptomatic neonate (jitteriness, lethargy, poor feeding, seizures), any glucose below the operational treatment threshold - under 40 mg/dL per AAP, or under 45 mg/dL per the Cornblath criteria widely used in Indian NICU protocols - warrants prompt IV dextrose (mini-bolus of 200 mg/kg, i.e. 2 mL/kg of 10% dextrose, followed by an infusion at 6-8 mg/kg/min glucose infusion rate) rather than watchful waiting, since untreated neonatal hypoglycemia risks neurological injury.

subject: Paediatrics
q: A 14-year-old unvaccinated boy develops bilateral parotid swelling followed 5 days later by unilateral testicular pain, swelling and tenderness. What is the most likely complication, and its typical timing relative to the parotitis?
opts: Epididymo-orchitis from a sexually transmitted infection, unrelated to the parotid swelling
Testicular torsion, a coincidental surgical emergency
Mumps orchitis, typically occurring 4-8 days after onset of parotitis, usually post-pubertal
why: The temporal association with parotitis in an unvaccinated adolescent strongly points to mumps, not an unrelated STI.
Torsion is an acute vascular emergency unrelated temporally to parotitis, not fitting this sequential story.
Correct - mumps orchitis typically follows parotitis by 4-8 days in post-pubertal males.
A tumour would not present acutely with pain/swelling temporally linked to parotitis.
exp: Mumps orchitis is the most common extra-salivary complication of mumps in post-pubertal males, typically appearing about 4-8 days after parotitis onset; it is usually unilateral and can cause testicular atrophy, but rarely causes infertility since bilateral involvement is uncommon.

subject: Paediatrics
q: An 18-month-old with fever has a seizure lasting 25 minutes with clonic jerking confined to the left arm, and a second similar seizure occurs 4 hours later during the same illness. How should this seizure be classified, and what does the classification prompt?
opts: Simple febrile seizure - reassurance and discharge only
Breakthrough epilepsy - start maintenance antiepileptics immediately
Febrile status epilepticus only if it exceeds 60 minutes, otherwise simple
Complex febrile seizure (focal, prolonged over 15 minutes, and recurrent within 24 hours) - warrants further evaluation for an underlying cause
why: This seizure meets multiple complex-feature criteria, so calling it simple understates the need for further workup.
A single febrile seizure episode, even complex, does not equate to a diagnosis of epilepsy nor mandate immediate maintenance antiepileptics.
The defining criteria are 15-minute duration, focality and recurrence - not a 60-minute cutoff - and 25 minutes already qualifies.
Correct - focal onset, duration over 15 minutes, and recurrence within 24 hours together define a complex febrile seizure.
exp: A febrile seizure is classified as complex if it has any one of: focal onset/features, duration over 15 minutes, or recurrence within 24 hours of the same febrile illness - this case has all three, and complex febrile seizures carry a higher likelihood of an identifiable underlying neurological process warranting further evaluation.

subject: Paediatrics
q: A 6-year-old presents with polyuria (>4 mL/kg/hr), extreme thirst, and dilute urine (specific gravity 1.001) despite a serum sodium of 148 mEq/L. Which test would best confirm the suspected diagnosis?
opts: Water deprivation test with subsequent desmopressin administration
why: Correct - failure to concentrate urine on deprivation, followed by response to desmopressin, confirms central DI.
Relevant to adrenal insufficiency workups, not this polyuria-hypernatremia picture.
Helps distinguish causes of hyponatremia, not this hypernatremic dilute-urine picture.
Used in acute kidney injury workup (prerenal vs intrinsic), not relevant here.
exp: The combination of inappropriately dilute urine despite hypernatremia/high serum osmolality suggests diabetes insipidus; a water deprivation test followed by desmopressin administration distinguishes central DI (urine then concentrates) from nephrogenic DI (urine stays dilute despite desmopressin).

subject: Paediatrics
q: A previously healthy 8-year-old develops jaundice, altered sensorium, and a prothrombin time markedly prolonged and uncorrected by intravenous vitamin K, 5 days into a febrile illness. What is the diagnosis and the appropriate next step?
opts: Viral hepatitis with cholestasis - outpatient follow-up in 2 weeks
Pediatric acute liver failure - urgent referral to a liver transplant center
Reye syndrome - treat with aspirin taper
Biliary atresia - refer for Kasai portoenterostomy
why: These red-flag features (encephalopathy, vitamin K-unresponsive coagulopathy) mean this has evolved into liver failure, not simple hepatitis for outpatient follow-up.
Correct - coagulopathy uncorrected by vitamin K plus altered sensorium defines acute liver failure needing urgent transfer.
Reye syndrome is linked to aspirin use and presents with encephalopathy and elevated ammonia typically without significant jaundice; aspirin is the precipitant, never the treatment.
Biliary atresia presents in early infancy with persistent conjugated jaundice and acholic stools, not an acute presentation at age 8 with encephalopathy.
exp: Acute liver failure in a child is defined by biochemical evidence of liver injury with coagulopathy (INR/PT elevated and uncorrected by vitamin K), often with hepatic encephalopathy, in a patient without known chronic liver disease; this combination is a medical emergency requiring urgent transfer to a center capable of intensive/transplant care.

subject: Paediatrics
q: A 4-year-old boy with steroid-sensitive nephrotic syndrome, currently in relapse with severe anasarca and hemoconcentration, develops sudden-onset left flank pain, gross hematuria, and a newly palpable left-sided abdominal mass over 48 hours. Which complication of nephrotic syndrome is most likely?
why: Pyelonephritis presents with fever and dysuria or pyuria, not an acute mass with hematuria
Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis presents with fever, abdominal pain, and peritoneal signs, not flank pain and a renal mass
Wilms tumor is typically a slower-growing, painless mass, not an acute 48-hour event with hematuria
Correct - nephrotic syndrome's hypercoagulable state predisposes to renal vein thrombosis
exp: Nephrotic syndrome causes a hypercoagulable state via urinary loss of antithrombin III, hemoconcentration, and thrombocytosis - renal vein thrombosis is the classic vascular complication presenting with acute flank pain, gross hematuria, and renal enlargement, prompting urgent renal Doppler or CT imaging.

subject: Paediatrics
q: A term neonate born by vaginal delivery is apneic and floppy at birth with a heart rate of 80 per minute despite thorough drying, stimulation, and 30 seconds of effective positive pressure ventilation with visible chest rise. As per the NRP algorithm, what is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Continue effective positive pressure ventilation and reassess the heart rate after 15 seconds before escalating
Discontinue resuscitation as the heart rate is adequate
why: Correct - with heart rate 60-100 and ventilation already effective, the next step is to continue that ventilation and reassess shortly, not escalate
Epinephrine is reserved for heart rate below 60 despite effective PPV plus chest compressions
Chest compressions are indicated only when heart rate stays below 60 despite 30 seconds of effective PPV, which is not yet the case here
A heart rate of 80 is inadequate, target is above 100, so resuscitation must continue
exp: In the NRP algorithm, chest compressions begin only when heart rate stays below 60 per minute after 30 seconds of effective PPV with confirmed chest rise - a heart rate of 60-100 with ventilation already effective calls for continuing that ventilation and reassessing shortly, not premature escalation to compressions or epinephrine.

subject: Paediatrics
q: A 6-year-old child from a rural agricultural area presents with high-grade fever for 8 days, unresponsive to empirical antimalarials and antibiotics, along with a painless black eschar in the axilla and hepatosplenomegaly. Which diagnosis best fits this presentation?
why: Enteric fever does not classically produce an eschar, and presents with stepladder fever and relative bradycardia
Correct - the pathognomonic painless eschar at the mite-bite site fits scrub typhus
Dengue presents with thrombocytopenia, rash, and warning signs, not an eschar
Leptospirosis presents with conjunctival suffusion, myalgia, and jaundice or acute kidney injury, not an eschar
exp: The pathognomonic eschar, a painless black necrotic crusted lesion at the chigger mite bite site, in a prolonged fever unresponsive to routine antimalarials and antibiotics should immediately suggest scrub typhus - treat empirically with doxycycline given the mortality risk of untreated disease.

subject: Paediatrics
q: A 10-year-old known type 1 diabetic presents with vomiting, abdominal pain, and Kussmaul breathing. Blood glucose is 350 mg/dL, venous pH 7.15, serum bicarbonate 8 mEq/L, and urine ketones 3+. As per ISPAD criteria, how should this episode of diabetic ketoacidosis be classified?
opts: Impending DKA, not yet meeting criteria
why: Mild DKA requires pH below 7.3 or bicarbonate below 15, a milder derangement than this case
Biochemical criteria for established DKA, ketonuria, hyperglycemia, and acidosis, are already met
Correct - ISPAD defines moderate DKA as pH below 7.2 and bicarbonate below 10, matching this case
Severe DKA requires pH below 7.1 and bicarbonate below 5, which this case does not reach
exp: ISPAD grades DKA severity by venous pH and bicarbonate: mild is pH below 7.3 or bicarbonate below 15, moderate is pH below 7.2 with bicarbonate below 10, and severe is pH below 7.1 with bicarbonate below 5 - grading drives fluid rate and monitoring intensity given the cerebral edema risk during correction.

subject: Paediatrics
q: A 7-year-old child with bacterial meningitis develops hyponatremia with serum sodium 122 mEq/L on day 3. She has high urine output, markedly elevated urine sodium, dry mucous membranes, and tachycardia suggesting volume depletion. Which condition best explains this, and how is it distinguished from SIADH?
opts: SIADH, distinguished by the child being clinically euvolemic to hypervolemic with concentrated urine
Diabetes insipidus, distinguished by dilute urine and hypernatremia
Cerebral salt wasting, distinguished by clinical hypovolemia despite natriuresis and hyponatremia
Adrenal insufficiency, distinguished by hyperkalemia and hypotension without natriuresis
why: SIADH patients are euvolemic to hypervolemic, not dehydrated, which does not match this vignette
Diabetes insipidus causes hypernatremia with dilute urine, the opposite picture to this hyponatremic case
Correct - cerebral salt wasting causes renal sodium wasting with true volume depletion and hyponatremia
Adrenal insufficiency would show hyperkalemia and hypotension without this natriuretic pattern
exp: Cerebral salt wasting and SIADH can both cause hyponatremia in a child with CNS infection or injury, but demand opposite treatment - CSW needs salt and volume replacement since the patient is volume-depleted, while SIADH needs fluid restriction since the patient is volume-expanded, so bedside volume status assessment is the key discriminator before choosing therapy.

subject: Paediatrics
q: A newborn is delivered with a ventral abdominal wall defect. Bowel loops herniate through an opening to the right of a normally inserted, intact umbilical cord, with no covering sac, and the exposed bowel appears edematous and matted. Which condition is this, and how does its associated-anomaly rate differ from the main alternative?
opts: Gastroschisis, typically an isolated defect with a low rate of associated chromosomal or cardiac anomalies, unlike omphalocele
Omphalocele, typically has a covering sac and a high rate of associated anomalies
Umbilical hernia, a benign midline defect covered by skin, resolving spontaneously
Bladder exstrophy, a lower midline defect involving the urinary bladder
why: Correct - gastroschisis is a paraumbilical, sac-less defect that is usually isolated with low anomaly rates
Omphalocele is midline through the umbilical ring with an intact sac, not matching this off-midline sac-less description
Umbilical hernia is an unrelated small skin-covered defect
Bladder exstrophy involves exposed bladder mucosa, not herniated bowel loops beside the cord
exp: The key differentiator between gastroschisis and omphalocele is anatomic, a paraumbilical defect with no sac versus a midline defect through the cord with an intact sac, and prognostic, since gastroschisis is usually isolated needing prompt bowel protection and surgery, while omphalocele warrants a careful search for associated cardiac, chromosomal, and Beckwith-Wiedemann spectrum anomalies.

subject: Paediatrics
q: A 14-year-old boy presents with complete absence of pubertal development, Tanner stage 1 genitalia, testicular volume 2 mL bilaterally, short stature relative to family, and lifelong anosmia. Which diagnosis best explains this combination?
opts: Constitutional delay of growth and puberty
why: Constitutional delay is a diagnosis of exclusion in an otherwise well child and does not explain anosmia
Correct - Kallmann syndrome is isolated hypogonadotropic hypogonadism from defective GnRH neuron migration alongside olfactory bulb hypoplasia
Klinefelter syndrome shows small firm testes, gynecomastia, and tall stature, not anosmia
Isolated growth hormone deficiency causes short stature with delayed bone age but not anosmia or this degree of pubertal arrest
exp: Anosmia plus delayed or absent puberty in a boy is the classic clue to Kallmann syndrome, caused by failure of GnRH neuron migration together with olfactory bulb maldevelopment - confirm with low LH and FSH, low testosterone, and MRI showing olfactory bulb hypoplasia, then treat with pubertal induction using testosterone or pulsatile GnRH.

subject: Paediatrics
q: A 9-month-old with acute gastroenteritis has been rehydrated and is now on maintenance IV fluids. Six hours later he develops a generalised tonic-clonic seizure; serum sodium is 118 mEq/L. What is the most likely cause of this seizure?
opts: Too-rapid correction of a pre-existing hypernatremia
Febrile seizure unrelated to the fluid therapy
Hypocalcemia secondary to citrate in the IV fluid
Hospital-acquired hyponatremia from hypotonic maintenance fluid plus non-osmotic ADH release
why: Wrong direction — this child was hyponatremic, not hypernatremic
The biochemistry (Na 118) makes hyponatremic seizure far more likely than a coincidental febrile seizure
Citrate load is not a recognised cause of acute symptomatic hypocalcemia here
Correct — classic hospital-acquired hyponatremia mechanism
exp: Sick children secrete ADH non-osmotically; giving hypotonic maintenance fluid in this state causes free-water retention and iatrogenic hyponatremic seizures - isotonic maintenance fluid is now preferred in acutely ill children (NICE CG174).

subject: Paediatrics
q: A 6-week-old exclusively breastfed infant has progressive non-bilious vomiting after feeds for 5 days, now with visible peristaltic waves and a palpable olive in the right upper quadrant. Venous blood gas shows pH 7.52, HCO3 32, Cl 88. What is the single best initial step before any surgery is planned?
opts: Emergency pyloromyotomy within 6 hours to prevent perforation
Nasogastric decompression alone, then discharge once vomiting stops
Upper GI contrast study to confirm the string sign before any fluid therapy
Correction of the hypochloremic, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis with IV normal saline and potassium
why: Surgery is elective after resuscitation, never rushed
Decompression alone does not correct the metabolic derangement or treat the obstruction
Imaging/USG can wait for and follow resuscitation, not precede it
Correct - resuscitate first, always
exp: In infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis, surgery is never an emergency - correct the hypochloremic hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis first, because anaesthetising an alkalotic infant risks post-operative apnoea.

subject: Paediatrics
q: A 4-year-old girl's height is plotted well below the 3rd centile with a growth velocity that has been flat for the past 18 months, while her weight-for-height remains normal. Which single next investigation is most useful to distinguish a primary growth disorder from constitutional causes?
opts: Karyotype in every short girl regardless of other features
why: Random GH is unreliable (pulsatile secretion) and not the first test

Karyotype is actually indicated in any girl with unexplained short stature regardless of dysmorphic features (to rule out Turner syndrome) - but it screens for a specific chromosomal cause and does not by itself distinguish a constitutional growth pattern from a pathological one, which is what this stem is asking
IGF-1 is useful but interpreted alongside bone age, not alone
Correct - bone age vs chronological/height age is the standard triage step
exp: A flat growth velocity points away from familial short stature towards a pathological cause; comparing bone age to chronological/height age is the standard first discriminator in a short-stature workup.

subject: Paediatrics
q: A 7-year-old boy has early-morning vomiting, worsening headache over 3 weeks, and new-onset diplopia on lateral gaze. Fundoscopy shows bilateral papilledema. Which cranial nerve finding is explained purely by raised intracranial pressure rather than the tumour's direct location?
opts: Facial nerve palsy from cerebellopontine angle involvement
Third nerve palsy from direct brainstem compression
Sixth nerve (abducens) palsy as a false localising sign
Optic atrophy from direct optic nerve infiltration
why: CPA involvement would be a true localising sign of a specific posterior fossa lesion
Third nerve palsy from uncal herniation is a true localising sign, not this mechanism
Correct - classic false localising sign of raised ICP
Optic atrophy here follows papilledema (raised ICP), it is not direct infiltration
exp: The abducens nerve has the longest intracranial course and is most vulnerable to stretch from raised ICP anywhere in the skull, producing a false localising sixth nerve palsy that does not indicate the tumour's actual site.

subject: Paediatrics
q: A term neonate born by vacuum-assisted delivery develops a boggy scalp swelling that crosses suture lines and is present at birth, gradually increasing in size over the first day. There is no skull fracture. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why: Cephalhematoma is subperiosteal so it is strictly limited by suture lines
Caput is present at birth but pits on pressure and resolves within days without progressive expansion
Correct - crosses sutures, expands after birth, vacuum-associated
Cutis marmorata is a vasomotor skin mottling, not a scalp swelling
exp: Subgaleal hemorrhage bleeds into the potential space between galea aponeurotica and periosteum, so it is not limited by suture lines and keeps expanding - it carries real risk of hypovolemic shock, so serial head circumference and hematocrit monitoring are mandatory after vacuum delivery.

subject: Paediatrics
q: A 3-year-old unimmunized child presents with fever, a barking cough, and inspiratory stridor at rest. Despite nebulized adrenaline and steroids he remains stridulous at rest with intercostal recession. What is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Discharge home with oral steroids since he is unimmunized and likely just has severe croup
Repeat nebulized adrenaline every 15 minutes indefinitely at home
IV antibiotics alone, as this is bacterial tracheitis until proven otherwise
Immediate ENT/anaesthesia-assisted airway assessment with readiness for intubation
why: A child with red-flag signs despite treatment must not be discharged
Repeating adrenaline without escalation ignores treatment failure
Bacterial tracheitis is a differential but the immediate priority given red flags is airway readiness
Correct - treatment failure in croup needs airway backup, not more nebulisation at home
exp: Persistent at-rest stridor and recession despite adequate treatment defines severe/impending-failure croup, which mandates a secured airway pathway with anaesthesia/ENT on standby.

subject: Paediatrics
q: A 5-year-old known asthmatic on regular inhaled budesonide develops acute severe breathlessness. On examination the chest is silent with no wheeze audible, respiratory rate is falling, and he is becoming drowsy. What does the silent chest with falling respiratory rate indicate?
opts: Improving asthma as airflow obstruction is resolving
Adequate response to bronchodilators, ready for stepping down therapy
Foreign body aspiration is now confirmed
Life-threatening asthma with critically reduced air entry, not clinical improvement
why: A silent chest is a danger sign, never a sign of improvement
Falling respiratory rate with drowsiness is exhaustion, not response to treatment
Foreign body is a differential in acute wheeze but this picture in a known asthmatic points to severe attack
Correct - classic life-threatening asthma feature
exp: A silent chest in acute asthma means air movement is too poor to generate wheeze; combined with falling respiratory rate and drowsiness (CO2 narcosis/exhaustion), this is life-threatening asthma requiring immediate escalation.

subject: Paediatrics
q: A term neonate delivered by difficult vaginal delivery with shoulder dystocia and prolonged lateral traction on the head has an adducted, internally rotated left arm, extended elbow, pronated forearm, and absent Moro reflex on that side, with an intact grasp reflex. Which nerve roots are most likely injured?
why: Correct — C5-C6 root injury from lateral traction produces the classic waiter's tip posture with intact hand grasp
Klumpke's involves C8-T1, causing a claw hand with absent grasp reflex (sometimes Horner syndrome), which this baby does not have
Phrenic nerve palsy (C3-5) causes diaphragmatic paralysis/respiratory distress, not this arm posture
Isolated C7 wrist drop is not a recognized obstetric plexus pattern; C7 is only involved in a total (C5-T1) palsy
exp: Erb-Duchenne palsy (C5-C6, upper trunk) is the commonest obstetric brachial plexus injury, classically after shoulder dystocia/macrosomic delivery with lateral neck traction — waiter's tip posture (arm adducted, internally rotated, elbow extended, forearm pronated) but grasp reflex preserved. Distinguishes it from Klumpke's (C8-T1) where the hand/grasp is affected. Most recover spontaneously within 3 months with physiotherapy; refer for surgical exploration if no biceps recovery by 3-6 months.

subject: Paediatrics
q: A neonate born to a mother who had an unimmunized febrile illness with rash in the first trimester of pregnancy presents with bilateral cataracts, a continuous machinery murmur, and sensorineural hearing loss on the newborn hearing screen. Which is the most likely underlying congenital infection?
why: CMV is the commonest congenital infection overall but classically causes microcephaly, periventricular calcification, and blueberry-muffin rash, not the cataract-PDA-deafness triad
Correct — this is Gregg's triad of congenital rubella
Toxoplasmosis gives chorioretinitis, hydrocephalus, and diffuse intracranial calcification, not cataract/PDA
Syphilis gives snuffles, saddle nose, and later Hutchinson teeth, not this triad
exp: Gregg's triad of congenital rubella syndrome is cataract (or other eye defects), congenital heart disease (PDA is most common), and sensorineural hearing loss. Risk and severity are highest with maternal infection in the first trimester. Universal MMR/MR immunization and antenatal screening are the prevention strategy.

subject: Paediatrics
q: A 6-year-old with known recurrent wheeze presents with severe breathlessness, use of accessory muscles, inability to speak in full sentences, and oxygen saturation of 88% on room air. Which finding on chest auscultation is the most ominous indicator of impending respiratory failure?
opts: Silent chest with poor air entry
why: Loud wheeze throughout the chest actually indicates some air movement, making it less severe than a silent chest
Tachypnea at 40/min signals distress but is not by itself life-threatening compared to a silent chest
Correct — a silent chest means almost no air is moving, the most ominous sign
Mild subcostal retractions indicate only mild-to-moderate work of breathing
exp: In acute severe asthma, a silent chest (poor air entry, wheeze may disappear) signals critical airway obstruction and impending respiratory failure — a red-flag sign requiring immediate escalation (nebulized bronchodilators, IV magnesium sulfate/steroids, PICU consult), not reassurance that the wheeze has resolved.

subject: Paediatrics
q: On routine newborn examination of a female infant born breech at term, the hip is flexed and adducted, and gentle posterior pressure produces a palpable clunk as the femoral head dislocates out of the acetabulum. Which clinical test does this describe, and what is the next best step?
opts: Ortolani test; refer for hip ultrasound
Galeazzi sign; obtain pelvic X-ray immediately
Trendelenburg test; start Pavlik harness without imaging
Barlow test; refer for hip ultrasound
why: Ortolani is the reduction maneuver (abduction, clunk of reduction), the opposite direction from what is described
Galeazzi sign assesses limb-length/knee-height discrepancy, not a dislocation provocation test, and X-ray is not first-line under 4-6 months
Trendelenburg is a standing/gait test used in walking children, not a newborn exam finding, and harness should follow confirmation
Correct — this is the Barlow maneuver; ultrasound confirms before starting Pavlik harness
exp: Barlow test provokes/dislocates an unstable hip (flexion, adduction, posterior pressure); Ortolani test instead reduces an already-dislocated hip. Breech presentation, female sex, and family history are the classic DDH risk factors. Hip ultrasound (not X-ray, since the femoral head is unossified cartilage before 4-6 months) is the imaging of choice; Pavlik harness follows confirmed diagnosis.

subject: Paediatrics
q: An exclusively breastfed 6-week-old infant is thriving and gaining weight well but passes small streaks of fresh blood mixed with mucus in otherwise normal stools, with no fever, vomiting, or abdominal distension. Which is the most likely diagnosis and first-line management?
opts: Food protein-induced allergic proctocolitis; maternal dietary elimination of cow's milk protein
Intussusception; urgent ultrasound and pneumatic reduction
why: Correct — the classic picture of a well, thriving infant with isolated rectal bleeding
Intussusception presents with paroxysmal colic, vomiting, and later currant-jelly stools in an ill-looking infant, not a well thriving one
Hirschsprung presents with delayed meconium passage/chronic constipation, not bloody stools in a thriving infant
Infectious colitis usually has fever/systemic illness, and antibiotics are not first-line without a confirmed pathogen
exp: Food protein-induced allergic (non-IgE-mediated) proctocolitis presents in an otherwise well, thriving breastfed infant with blood/mucus-streaked stools and no systemic illness. First-line management in a breastfed infant is maternal elimination of cow's milk protein (and often soy), not stopping breastfeeding. Most infants outgrow this by 1-2 years.

subject: Paediatrics
q: A 6-year-old boy has height persistently below the 3rd percentile with a growth velocity of less than 4 cm/year over the past two years, a bone age of 4 years, normal thyroid function, and normal body proportions. Which investigation best confirms the suspected diagnosis?
opts: Insulin-like growth factor-1 (IGF-1) and GH stimulation test
Serum calcium and vitamin D levels
why: Karyotype (for Turner syndrome) is relevant in short girls, not this boy with delayed bone age
Correct — the confirmatory work-up for suspected GH deficiency
Calcium/vitamin D would assess rickets, which usually shows bony deformities, not isolated short stature
Anti-tTG screens for celiac disease, usually accompanied by GI symptoms, not this isolated pattern
exp: Height below 3rd percentile with growth velocity under 4 cm/year and bone age delayed by more than 2 years, after excluding hypothyroidism, celiac disease, and chronic illness, raises suspicion for growth hormone deficiency. Because GH secretion is pulsatile, diagnosis requires low IGF-1/IGFBP-3 plus a GH stimulation test showing failure of GH rise; confirmed cases need pituitary MRI before starting recombinant GH.

subject: Paediatrics
q: A 3-year-old boy presents with periorbital puffiness progressing to generalized pitting edema over one week, urine dipstick showing 4+ proteinuria, serum albumin 1.8 g/dL, normal blood pressure, normal renal function, and normal serum complement (C3). Which is the most likely diagnosis and expected response to treatment?
opts: Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis; spontaneous resolution without steroids
Membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis; typically steroid-resistant with low C3
Minimal change disease; expected to be steroid-responsive
IgA nephropathy; managed with ACE inhibitors alone
why: PSGN classically has hematuria, hypertension, and low C3, not nephrotic-range proteinuria with normal C3/BP, and isn't steroid-treated
MPGN classically has persistently low C3 and is often steroid-resistant, unlike this normal-C3 picture
Correct — the classic steroid-sensitive nephrotic syndrome of childhood
IgA nephropathy usually presents with recurrent hematuria, not nephrotic syndrome, and isn't managed with ACEi alone acutely
exp: Minimal change disease accounts for 80-90% of idiopathic nephrotic syndrome in children aged 1-10 years: normotensive, normal renal function, normal complement, and characteristically steroid-responsive (over 90% remit with an 8-12 week course of oral prednisolone). Renal biopsy is reserved for atypical features (age under 1 or over 10, hematuria, hypertension, low complement, steroid resistance).

subject: Paediatrics
q: A 4-year-old admitted with pneumonia is prescribed maintenance intravenous fluids for 48 hours while tolerating nothing orally. Current evidence favours which fluid choice to reduce the risk of hospital-acquired hyponatremia?
why: Traditional hypotonic Holliday-Segar fluids raise hyponatremia risk in acutely unwell children with non-osmotic ADH secretion.
Plain dextrose has no sodium at all, the worst option for hyponatremia risk.
Half-strength Darrow's is still hypotonic relative to plasma.
Correct - isotonic maintenance fluid is now the preferred default for most hospitalized children to reduce hyponatremia risk.
exp: Sick hospitalized children secrete ADH non-osmotically (pain, nausea, illness), impairing free-water excretion; giving hypotonic maintenance fluid on top of this predisposes to dangerous acute hyponatremia, which is why isotonic fluid is now the safer default beyond the neonatal period.

subject: Paediatrics
q: A 5-week-old first-born male presents with progressively worsening non-bilious projectile vomiting after every feed, remains hungry after vomiting, and has a palpable olive-shaped mass in the right upper quadrant. Which acid-base and electrolyte pattern is expected?
why: Correct - loss of HCl-rich gastric contents causes hypochloremia and bicarbonate retention, while volume depletion drives aldosterone-mediated renal K+/H+ wasting.
Loss of gastric acid causes alkalosis, not acidosis.
Doesn't fit isolated vomiting losses.
Respiratory alkalosis is unrelated to this GI loss pattern.
exp: Hypertrophic pyloric stenosis classically produces hypochloremic, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis with paradoxical aciduria; fluid and electrolyte correction must precede pyloromyotomy, and diagnosis is confirmed on ultrasound (pyloric wall thickness and channel length).

subject: Paediatrics
q: A father is 175 cm tall and a mother is 155 cm tall. Using the standard formula, what is the calculated mid-parental (target) height for their son, and which diagnosis would this help rule in if the boy's height is tracking well below the resulting target-height range?
opts: 160 cm; consistent with familial short stature only if child's height matches this value
172 cm; a height persistently far below this target range supports a pathological rather than familial cause
155 cm; child should be evaluated only if taller than this
165 cm; irrelevant once bone age is known
why: Miscalculates the target height and its interpretation.
Correct - mid-parental height for a boy = (father's + mother's height)/2 + 6.5 cm = 172 cm; a height persistently well below this range points to a pathological rather than familial cause.
Uses only the mother's height, ignoring the formula.
Dismisses a clinically useful screening tool.
exp: Mid-parental height gives a quick target-height range for a child; tracking within about 8-10 cm of it supports familial short stature, while falling well below it (especially with declining growth velocity) should trigger work-up for an endocrine, chronic-disease, or syndromic cause rather than reassurance.

subject: Paediatrics
q: A 6-month-old has clusters of sudden flexor spasms of the neck, trunk and limbs occurring in series, especially on waking, with regression of the previously acquired social smile. EEG shows a chaotic, high-voltage disorganized background. Which diagnosis and first-line therapy fit best?
opts: Febrile seizure; no maintenance therapy needed
West syndrome (infantile spasms) with hypsarrhythmia; ACTH or vigabatrin
why: Rolandic epilepsy is a benign focal epilepsy of older children with nocturnal facial seizures, a different age and semiology.
Febrile seizures occur with fever and do not cause developmental regression or hypsarrhythmia.
Correct - the triad of infantile spasms, regression, and hypsarrhythmia at 3-8 months defines West syndrome; first-line therapy is ACTH or vigabatrin.
Lennox-Gastaut presents later (1-8 years) with multiple seizure types and a slow spike-wave pattern, not hypsarrhythmia.
exp: West syndrome must be recognized and treated promptly (ACTH or vigabatrin) because delay in controlling the spasms worsens the long-term developmental outcome - a paediatric neurology emergency of sorts, not just another seizure type.

subject: Paediatrics
q: A term neonate, exclusively breastfed, is noted to have visible jaundice extending to the palms and soles on day 4 of life, with total serum bilirubin at the phototherapy threshold for age on the standard nomogram. What is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Reassure and review only if jaundice worsens
Stop breastfeeding and switch to formula only
Start intensive phototherapy and monitor bilirubin trend
why: Underestimates the risk at this threshold.
Exchange transfusion is reserved for levels far above the phototherapy threshold or with signs of acute bilirubin encephalopathy.
Breastfeeding is not stopped for physiologic/breastfeeding-associated jaundice at this stage.
Correct - jaundice to the palms/soles at the age-specific phototherapy threshold warrants starting intensive phototherapy and rechecking the bilirubin trend.
exp: Cephalocaudal progression of jaundice to the palms/soles is a rough bedside clue to a higher bilirubin level; combined with a level at the nomogram's phototherapy threshold, it should prompt starting treatment rather than watchful waiting, to prevent progression toward kernicterus risk.

subject: Paediatrics
q: A 7-year-old with day 4 of high fever now has defervescence but develops persistent vomiting, abdominal pain, and lethargy, with a rising hematocrit on repeat testing. Which of these is a recognized dengue warning sign requiring close in-hospital monitoring?
opts: Persistent vomiting with rising hematocrit around defervescence
Mild headache with normal platelet count
Rash appearing on day 1 of fever
why: Correct - WHO dengue warning signs, appearing around defervescence when plasma-leak risk peaks, include persistent vomiting, abdominal pain, lethargy, and a rising hematocrit.
Dengue fever classically resolves by day 5-7; prolonged fever alone is not a listed warning sign.
Normal platelets and mild headache are reassuring, not warning features.
Rash timing alone is not a warning sign.
exp: The transition around defervescence (day 3-7) is the highest-risk window for plasma leakage in dengue; warning signs at this point (vomiting, abdominal pain, lethargy, rising hematocrit with falling platelets, bleeding, hepatomegaly) mandate hospitalization even if the child looks otherwise well.

subject: Paediatrics
q: A term neonate develops respiratory distress within minutes of birth, with a scaphoid abdomen, absent breath sounds on the left chest, and bowel sounds audible in the left hemithorax. Chest X-ray shows bowel loops in the thoracic cavity with mediastinal shift to the right. What is the immediate priority in resuscitation?
opts: Avoid bag-mask ventilation; secure the airway with endotracheal intubation and orogastric decompression
why: Bag-mask ventilation distends the herniated bowel with air, worsening lung compression, and is contraindicated in suspected CDH.
Correct - intubate promptly and place an orogastric tube on continuous suction to decompress the gut before gentle ventilation.
Nasal cannula oxygen does not secure the airway or decompress the gut in this degree of distress.
The mediastinal shift here is from herniated bowel, not a pneumothorax; thoracocentesis could injure bowel.
exp: In congenital diaphragmatic hernia, bag-mask ventilation is specifically avoided because it insufflates the herniated bowel and worsens the pulmonary hypoplasia/compression - early intubation with gut decompression is the resuscitation priority before any imaging confirms the diagnosis.

subject: Paediatrics
q: A 6-year-old, two weeks after a diarrheal illness, develops progressive symmetric ascending weakness starting in the legs, with absent deep tendon reflexes but preserved sensation and bladder function. CSF shows high protein with normal cell count. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why: Transverse myelitis usually causes a sensory level and early bladder involvement, not this pattern.
Poliomyelitis causes asymmetric flaccid paralysis and is now vanishingly rare in India post-eradication.
Correct - post-infectious ascending flaccid weakness with areflexia and CSF albuminocytologic dissociation defines Guillain-Barre syndrome.
Myasthenic crisis causes fatigable weakness with normal reflexes and normal CSF.
exp: Guillain-Barre syndrome, often triggered by a preceding Campylobacter jejuni diarrheal illness, produces symmetric ascending weakness with areflexia and a CSF albuminocytologic dissociation (high protein, normal cell count) - watch for respiratory muscle involvement, which determines the need for ICU monitoring.

subject: Paediatrics
q: A 3-year-old boy has had fever for 6 days along with bilateral non-purulent conjunctival injection, a strawberry tongue with cracked lips, a polymorphous rash, erythema and swelling of the hands and feet, and a single enlarged cervical lymph node. Which investigation is most important to screen for a serious complication of this condition?
opts: Throat swab for group A streptococcus
2D-echocardiography to screen for coronary artery aneurysms
why: Throat swab would be relevant for scarlet fever, which this presentation does not fit
Correct — screens for the complication that determines morbidity/mortality
Atypical lymphocytes suggest infectious mononucleosis, not Kawasaki disease
Uveitis screening is relevant to juvenile idiopathic arthritis workup, not the acute complication here
exp: This presentation meets the classic clinical criteria for Kawasaki disease; 2D-echocardiography is essential to detect coronary artery aneurysms, its most serious and potentially fatal complication, and prompt IVIG plus aspirin reduces this risk substantially.

subject: Paediatrics
q: An 8-month-old infant brought with cough and fever is found to have a respiratory rate of 54 breaths/min on repeated counting. As per WHO/IMNCI criteria, at what respiratory rate cutoff is 'fast breathing' defined for an infant in the 2 months to 12 months age group?
why: This is the correct cutoff for the 1-5 year age band, not 2-12 months
Correct cutoff for the 2 months-12 months age band, matching this infant
This is the cutoff for infants under 2 months
This rate does not correspond to any standard IMNCI age-band cutoff
exp: WHO/IMNCI defines age-specific fast-breathing cutoffs: ≥60/min for infants under 2 months, ≥50/min for infants 2 up to 12 months, and ≥40/min for children 1 to 5 years; applying the correct age-band cutoff is essential to correctly classify pneumonia under IMNCI.

subject: Paediatrics
q: A 4-year-old child admitted with moderate dehydration from acute gastroenteritis, now rehydrated, is prescribed intravenous maintenance fluids while oral intake is being re-established. As per current evidence-based recommendations, which type of maintenance fluid is now preferred over the traditionally used hypotonic fluids, to reduce the risk of hospital-acquired hyponatremia?
opts: Isotonic fluid — e.g., 0.9% saline (or a balanced isotonic solution) with appropriate dextrose
why: Correct as per current recommendations
This is the traditional approach now associated with hyponatremia risk
Hypertonic saline is used for symptomatic hyponatremia correction, not routine maintenance
Plain dextrose provides free water without electrolytes and worsens hyponatremia risk
exp: Traditional hypotonic maintenance fluids have been linked to hospital-acquired hyponatremia in sick, hospitalized children because non-osmotic ADH release impairs free-water excretion; current recommendations favour isotonic maintenance fluids for most hospitalized children. Practice still varies between institutions.

subject: Paediatrics
q: A female neonate presents on day 10 of life with vomiting, poor feeding, lethargy, hyponatremia and hyperkalemia. Examination reveals ambiguous genitalia with clitoromegaly and labial fusion. Which enzyme deficiency is most likely responsible for this presentation?
why: 11-beta-hydroxylase deficiency causes a non-salt-wasting, hypertensive form of CAH
17-alpha-hydroxylase deficiency causes hypertension with sexual infantilism, not salt-wasting virilization
17,20-lyase deficiency impairs androgen synthesis, causing undervirilization rather than virilization
Correct — the classic salt-wasting, virilizing form
exp: Classic salt-wasting congenital adrenal hyperplasia is most commonly caused by 21-hydroxylase deficiency, leading to cortisol and aldosterone deficiency (the salt-wasting crisis) with shunting of precursors toward androgen synthesis, causing virilization of female external genitalia.

subject: Paediatrics
q: A 12-year-old girl is noted to have breast budding — elevation of the breast and papilla as a small mound, with enlargement and separation of the areolar contours from the surrounding breast tissue — but no pubic hair yet. Which Tanner stage of breast development does this represent?
why: Stage 1 is prepubertal with no palpable glandular tissue, which does not match the budding described
Correct — matches the budding-with-areolar-separation description
Stage 3 shows further enlargement without contour separation between areola and breast
Stage 4 shows the areola and papilla projecting as a secondary mound above the breast contour
exp: Tanner stage 2 breast development (B2) is defined by breast budding with areolar enlargement — typically the first physical sign of puberty in girls, usually appearing between 8 and 13 years.

subject: Paediatrics
q: A 9-year-old boy develops gross hematuria within 24-48 hours of an upper respiratory tract infection. Serum complement (C3) levels are normal, and there is no significant latent period between the infection and the hematuria. Which glomerular disease is most consistent with this presentation, distinguishing it from post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis?
why: PSGN has a 10-14 day latent period and low C3, neither of which fit this vignette
Correct — matches the short latency and normal complement
Minimal change disease presents with nephrotic-range proteinuria/edema, not gross hematuria
Membranoproliferative GN typically shows persistently low complement, unlike this case
exp: IgA nephropathy classically presents with synpharyngitic gross hematuria — appearing within 24-48 hours of a respiratory or GI infection — with normal complement, in contrast to PSGN's 10-14 day latency and low C3 that normalizes by 6-8 weeks.

subject: Paediatrics
q: A term newborn with a history of a difficult delivery and low Apgar scores shows hyperalertness, mild hypotonia, and an exaggerated Moro reflex in the first 24 hours of life, with no seizures. Which stage of hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy (Sarnat staging) does this represent?
opts: This is normal neonatal behaviour, not HIE
why: Correct — matches hyperalertness plus mild hypotonia with no seizures
Stage 2 shows lethargy (not hyperalertness) and often seizures
Stage 3 shows coma/stupor and flaccidity, far more severe than described
The described findings, following documented perinatal asphyxia, do represent mild HIE, not normal behaviour
exp: Sarnat stage 1 (mild) HIE is characterized by hyperalertness, mild hypotonia, exaggerated primitive reflexes, and no seizures, usually resolving within 24 hours with a generally good prognosis. This is the original 1976 staging system widely taught in India — modified systems also exist.

subject: Paediatrics
q: A term neonate identified on newborn screening to have a markedly elevated TSH with low free T4 also has prolonged jaundice, a large posterior fontanelle, an umbilical hernia, and lethargy. Why is starting treatment within the first 2 weeks of life critical in this condition?
opts: To prevent irreversible neurodevelopmental delay/intellectual disability
why: Cardiac failure is not the primary concern driving urgency in congenital hypothyroidism
Correct — the time-critical rationale for early screening and treatment
Hepatosplenomegaly is not a feature this urgency addresses
Respiratory infection risk is not the key driver of treatment urgency here
exp: Thyroid hormone is essential for early brain myelination and neuronal maturation; delaying levothyroxine treatment for congenital hypothyroidism beyond the first 2 weeks of life risks irreversible intellectual disability, which is why universal newborn TSH screening and prompt treatment are strongly recommended.

subject: Paediatrics
q: A 6-week-old infant presents with inspiratory stridor that worsens on crying, feeding, and lying supine, but improves in the prone position, first noted around 2 weeks of age. There is no cyanosis, and the infant is feeding and growing well. What is the most likely diagnosis and its natural course?
opts: Croup (acute laryngotracheobronchitis); usually resolves within a week with steroids
Subglottic hemangioma; typically grows over months before involuting
Vascular ring; usually requires surgical correction
Laryngomalacia; most cases resolve spontaneously by 12-18 months of age
why: Croup is an acute infectious illness with a barking cough, not a chronic 4-week pattern like this
Subglottic hemangioma classically has a proliferative growth phase over months (worsening before improving), not a static chronic course from 2 weeks
Vascular rings often cause biphasic stridor with feeding difficulty and typically need surgery, not spontaneous resolution
Correct — matches the classic chronic, positional stridor pattern and natural history
exp: Laryngomalacia is the most common cause of chronic stridor in infancy; it typically begins in the first weeks of life, worsens with crying/feeding/supine positioning, improves prone, and resolves spontaneously in the large majority of infants by 12-18 months.

subject: Paediatrics
q: A 6-year-old child weighing 20 kg sustains 30% total body surface area burns. Using the paediatric-modified Parkland formula together with Holliday-Segar maintenance fluid, what is the correct total crystalloid fluid requirement for the first 24 hours?
opts: 2400 mL total (adult Parkland formula alone, no maintenance added)
1800 mL total (paediatric Parkland resuscitation volume alone, maintenance omitted)
3300 mL total -- 1800 mL paediatric Parkland resuscitation (half over the first 8 hours, remainder over the next 16 hours) plus 1500 mL Holliday-Segar maintenance
3900 mL total (adult Parkland formula plus maintenance)
why: Uses the adult 4 mL/kg/%TBSA multiplier and omits maintenance fluid entirely
Uses the correct paediatric 3 mL/kg/%TBSA resuscitation volume but forgets that children additionally need maintenance fluid
Correct -- paediatric-modified Parkland (3 mL/kg/%TBSA) plus Holliday-Segar maintenance, the current standard for children
Uses the adult 4 mL/kg/%TBSA multiplier with maintenance added, overestimating the resuscitation component
exp: In children the Parkland formula is modified to 3 mL x %TBSA x weight (kg) for resuscitation -- not the adult 4 mL/kg -- because the adult multiplier causes fluid-creep over-resuscitation in children; here 3x30x20 = 1800 mL, half over the first 8 hours and the rest over the next 16. This resuscitation volume excludes normal maintenance needs, so Holliday-Segar maintenance (100 mL/kg for the first 10 kg plus 50 mL/kg for the second 10 kg = 1500 mL/24h here) must be added separately, giving a 24-hour total of 3300 mL.

subject: Paediatrics
q: A 3-month-old exclusively breastfed infant has frequent, effortless regurgitation after most feeds, but is thriving well with normal weight gain, no respiratory symptoms, no feeding refusal, and no bilious or bloody vomiting. What is the most appropriate initial management?
opts: Start an empirical proton pump inhibitor
Reassurance and parental education; no investigation needed
why: PPIs are not indicated for uncomplicated physiological reflux in a thriving infant and are reserved for confirmed GERD with complications
Invasive pH-impedance monitoring is unnecessary without red-flag features
Endoscopy is reserved for suspected complications, absent here
Correct — the appropriate management of physiological 'happy spitting'
exp: Uncomplicated physiological gastroesophageal reflux (the 'happy spitter') in a thriving infant with no red-flag features requires only reassurance, parental education, and simple positioning/feeding advice; it typically resolves by 12-18 months as the lower oesophageal sphincter matures.

subject: Paediatrics
q: A macrosomic newborn delivered to a mother with poorly controlled gestational diabetes develops jitteriness, poor feeding, and a blood glucose of 30 mg/dL at 2 hours of life. What is the underlying pathophysiological mechanism for this neonatal hypoglycemia?
opts: Impaired glycogenolysis due to hepatic immaturity
Fetal hyperinsulinemia from chronic maternal hyperglycemia, causing rebound hypoglycemia after birth
Excess glucagon secretion from fetal pancreatic alpha cells
why: Hepatic glycogen stores are typically adequate in a macrosomic infant of a diabetic mother; the issue is excess insulin, not immature glycogenolysis
Correct — the fetal hyperinsulinemia mechanism
Adrenal insufficiency is not the mechanism in infants of diabetic mothers
Glucagon is not the driver; the pathology is beta-cell (insulin) excess, not alpha-cell excess
exp: Chronic maternal hyperglycemia drives fetal pancreatic beta-cell hyperplasia and hyperinsulinemia; after delivery, the maternal glucose supply is abruptly cut off but the infant's insulin remains elevated, driving rebound hypoglycemia — this is why infants of diabetic mothers require close glucose monitoring in the first hours of life.

subject: Paediatrics
q: A previously well 18-month-old boy develops sudden onset of coughing, choking, and gagging while eating groundnuts at home, followed by persistent unilateral wheeze on the right side. Chest X-ray shows hyperinflation of the right lung. What is the most likely diagnosis and the anatomical reason for the side involved?
opts: Asthma exacerbation; right lung is more reactive
Foreign body aspiration; the right main bronchus is wider, shorter, and more vertical than the left
Right-sided pneumothorax; due to a ruptured congenital bleb
why: Bronchiolitis presents with bilateral wheeze and a viral prodrome in infants, not sudden unilateral symptoms triggered by eating.
Asthma causes bilateral, diffuse wheeze, not a sudden, localized, choking-triggered unilateral episode, and "more reactive" lung sidedness is not a recognized concept.
Correct — the history and anatomy point clearly to foreign body aspiration lodging preferentially in the right main bronchus.
Pneumothorax would show a hyperlucent field without lung markings and mediastinal shift away from the affected side, not the choking-triggered onset described.
exp: Sudden-onset choking during eating followed by unilateral wheeze and localized hyperinflation (ball-valve effect) is classic for foreign body aspiration; the right main bronchus is wider, shorter, and more vertical than the left, so aspirated objects (including peanuts, a leading cause in toddlers) more commonly lodge on the right. Rigid bronchoscopy is diagnostic and therapeutic.

subject: Paediatrics
q: A malnourished 8-month-old infant with acute gastroenteritis was given only plain water at home by the family instead of ORS. She now presents lethargic with a generalized tonic-clonic seizure; serum sodium is 118 mEq/L. Which principle should guide correction of her hyponatremia?
opts: Correct slowly, raising serum sodium by no more than about 8–10 mEq/L in 24 hours, to avoid osmotic demyelination
Correct rapidly to normal sodium within 2–4 hours using 3% saline
Withhold all sodium-containing fluids until seizures stop
Give free water restriction alone without any sodium supplementation
why: Correct — slow, controlled correction (not exceeding roughly 8-10 mEq/L per 24h after initial seizure control) prevents osmotic demyelination.
Rapid full correction to normal within hours risks osmotic demyelination syndrome and is not recommended even for symptomatic hyponatremia beyond the initial seizure-aborting bolus.
Withholding all sodium delays correction of a genuinely dangerous electrolyte abnormality causing active seizures.
Free water restriction alone will not correct symptomatic hyponatremia with seizures — some hypertonic saline is needed acutely.
exp: Symptomatic hyponatremia (seizures) from excess free-water intake needs an initial small bolus of hypertonic (3%) saline to abort seizures, but overall correction must be limited to roughly 8-10 mEq/L in 24 hours — rapid correction of chronic/subacute hyponatremia risks osmotic demyelination, particularly dangerous in malnourished children.

subject: Paediatrics
q: A 9-year-old boy presents with a day's history of periumbilical pain that has now localized to the right iliac fossa, associated with anorexia, low-grade fever, and one episode of vomiting. On examination, there is tenderness and guarding at McBurney's point. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why: Mesenteric lymphadenitis often follows a viral URI and causes more diffuse abdominal tenderness without the classic migratory pain pattern described here.
Meckel's diverticulitis can mimic appendicitis but is far less common and does not have the same classic migratory pain pattern.
Intussusception typically presents with colicky pain, drawing up of legs, "redcurrant jelly" stools, and a sausage-shaped mass, not localized McBurney's point tenderness.
Correct — migratory periumbilical-to-RIF pain with McBurney's point tenderness is classic acute appendicitis.
exp: The classic sequence of vague periumbilical pain migrating to and localizing in the right iliac fossa, with anorexia, low-grade fever, and localized peritoneal signs at McBurney's point, is the textbook presentation of acute appendicitis — the most common surgical emergency in children beyond infancy.

subject: Paediatrics
q: An 18-month-old boy with a fever of 39.5°C due to a viral upper respiratory infection has a single generalized tonic-clonic seizure lasting 3 minutes, followed by full recovery within 20 minutes. He has no prior neurological history and a normal neurological examination. What is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Reassurance and counseling, with no need for EEG or neuroimaging
Lumbar puncture is mandatory in all cases
why: MRI is not indicated for a simple febrile seizure with a normal neurological exam and rapid recovery.
Correct — reassurance and parental counseling, without EEG/imaging, is standard management for a simple febrile seizure.
Maintenance antiepileptics are not indicated after a single simple febrile seizure, given the low recurrence risk of epilepsy.
Lumbar puncture is only indicated selectively — for infants under 12 months with incomplete immunization, those with meningeal signs, or where the picture suggests CNS infection, not in all cases.
exp: A simple febrile seizure is a generalized seizure lasting <15 minutes, occurring once in 24 hours, in a neurologically normal child aged 6 months to 5 years with fever but no CNS infection — it needs no EEG, neuroimaging, or antiepileptic therapy; management is reassurance, antipyretics for comfort, and parental education on seizure first-aid.

subject: Paediatrics
q: A neonate born after a pregnancy complicated by severe oligohydramnios is noted to have bilateral flank masses and respiratory distress at birth. Renal ultrasound shows bilaterally enlarged, diffusely echogenic kidneys with loss of corticomedullary differentiation and innumerable tiny cysts. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why: Multicystic dysplastic kidney is typically unilateral with grossly visible, non-communicating cysts of varying size, not the bilateral diffusely echogenic pattern described.
Wilms tumor presents later in childhood (median age 3-4 years) as a solitary, well-defined mass, not bilateral diffuse echogenic kidneys at birth with oligohydramnios.
Correct — bilateral enlarged echogenic kidneys, oligohydramnios, and neonatal respiratory distress is the classic ARPKD picture.
Simple renal cysts are usually solitary, well-defined, and rarely cause oligohydramnios or bilateral kidney enlargement.
exp: ARPKD (PKHD1 gene mutation, fibrocystin defect) classically presents in the neonatal period with bilaterally enlarged, echogenic kidneys showing innumerable tiny collecting-duct cysts and loss of corticomedullary differentiation; severe oligohydramnios from reduced fetal urine output leads to Potter sequence (pulmonary hypoplasia, characteristic facies, limb deformities) and often fatal neonatal respiratory distress, with congenital hepatic fibrosis appearing later.

subject: Paediatrics
q: A term infant delivered by elective lower-segment caesarean section develops mild respiratory distress — tachypnea, mild grunting, and subcostal retractions — within the first few hours of life. Chest X-ray shows prominent perihilar streaking and fluid in the horizontal fissure. Symptoms resolve completely by 48–72 hours with supportive oxygen alone. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why: Correct — the elective-caesarean history, mild self-limited course, and fissure-fluid CXR findings are classic for TTN.

RDS from surfactant deficiency occurs predominantly in preterm infants and shows a diffuse reticulogranular ("ground-glass") pattern with air bronchograms, typically worsening rather than resolving by 48-72 hours without surfactant/CPAP.
Meconium aspiration syndrome occurs with meconium-stained liquor and shows patchy infiltrates with hyperinflation, usually in post-term or distressed infants, not this benign self-limited picture.
Congenital pneumonia typically has risk factors like prolonged rupture of membranes or maternal fever, and does not resolve spontaneously within 48-72 hours without antibiotics.
exp: Transient tachypnea of the newborn results from delayed clearance of fetal lung fluid, classically after elective caesarean delivery (which bypasses the vaginal squeeze and catecholamine surge that normally help clear lung fluid); it presents with tachypnea/mild distress within hours, shows perihilar streaking and fissure fluid on CXR, and is self-limited, resolving within 48-72 hours with supportive oxygen.

subject: Paediatrics
q: An unvaccinated 4-year-old presents with 3 days of fever, cough, coryza, and red watery eyes, followed by small bluish-white spots on an erythematous base on the buccal mucosa opposite the molars. A day later, a maculopapular rash appears, starting at the hairline and spreading downward. What is the diagnosis?
why: Rubella causes a milder illness with postauricular/suboccipital lymphadenopathy and a rash without a preceding 3-Cs prodrome or Koplik spots.
Scarlet fever follows streptococcal pharyngitis with a sandpaper rash and strawberry tongue, not a coryzal prodrome with Koplik spots.
Roseola infantum (HHV-6) causes high fever for 3-5 days followed by rash appearing as the fever breaks, in infants typically under 2 years, without Koplik spots.
Correct — the 3 Cs prodrome, Koplik spots, and cephalocaudal rash are pathognomonic for measles.
exp: Measles presents with the classic prodrome of the "3 Cs" (cough, coryza, conjunctivitis) plus high fever, followed by pathognomonic Koplik spots 1-2 days before the rash, then a cephalocaudal maculopapular rash starting at the hairline — it remains an important vaccine-preventable cause of morbidity in unvaccinated Indian children.

subject: Paediatrics
q: A 4-year-old boy who started walking late is brought in because he "walks like a duck" and has difficulty climbing stairs. On examination, his calves appear unusually bulky, and when asked to rise from the floor, he uses his hands to walk up his own thighs to stand. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why: Spinal muscular atrophy type II presents with hypotonia and proximal weakness but typically without calf pseudohypertrophy, and children with SMA II never achieve independent walking.
Correct — waddling gait, calf pseudohypertrophy, and a positive Gowers' sign in a young boy is classic Duchenne muscular dystrophy.
Spastic diplegia from cerebral palsy shows increased tone, scissoring gait, and a static (non-progressive) course from birth, not progressive proximal weakness with calf pseudohypertrophy.
Guillain-Barré syndrome is an acute, ascending, areflexic flaccid paralysis following an infection, not a chronic history of delayed walking with calf hypertrophy.
