exp: Duchenne muscular dystrophy (X-linked recessive, dystrophin gene mutation) classically presents in boys aged 3-5 years with delayed walking, waddling gait, calf pseudohypertrophy (fibrofatty infiltration), and a positive Gowers' sign (climbing up the legs to stand). Creatine kinase is markedly elevated; genetic testing/muscle biopsy confirms the diagnosis.

subject: Paediatrics
q: A 6-year-old with acute kidney injury from severe dehydration has a serum potassium of 7.2 mEq/L, and the ECG shows peaked T waves with a widened QRS. What is the correct first step in management, before measures that actually lower total body potassium?
opts: IV calcium gluconate to stabilize the cardiac membrane
why: Kayexalate removes potassium from the body but acts slowly (hours) and does not address the immediate arrhythmia risk from membrane instability.

Salbutamol shifts potassium intracellularly and is a useful adjunct but does not stabilize the myocardium as rapidly or directly as calcium, and should not replace calcium as the first step with ECG changes present.
Correct — calcium gluconate is the immediate first step to stabilize the myocardium whenever hyperkalemia causes ECG changes.
Furosemide can help eliminate potassium via the kidneys but acts too slowly to address an immediate arrhythmia risk and is unreliable in acute kidney injury.
exp: In severe hyperkalemia with ECG changes, IV calcium gluconate is given first — it does not lower serum potassium but rapidly stabilizes the cardiac cell membrane, raising the threshold potential and reducing arrhythmia risk, buying time for potassium-lowering measures (insulin-glucose, salbutamol, then Kayexalate/diuretics/dialysis) to act.

subject: Paediatrics
q: An 11-year-old girl has 3 months of recurrent epigastric pain that often wakes her at night, partially relieved by food, along with mild pallor. Upper GI endoscopy shows antral gastritis with a duodenal ulcer, and a urease breath test is positive. What is the most appropriate treatment approach?
opts: H. pylori eradication triple therapy (proton pump inhibitor plus two antibiotics)
Dietary modification alone, with reassessment in 6 months
why: Correct — triple therapy (PPI plus two antibiotics) is standard for confirmed H. pylori-associated peptic ulcer disease.
PPI monotherapy heals the ulcer symptomatically but does not eradicate H. pylori, leading to high relapse rates.
There is no indication of a helminthic infection here; the breath test specifically confirms H. pylori, not worms.
Dietary modification alone will not eradicate a confirmed bacterial infection driving active ulcer disease.
exp: A positive urease breath test with endoscopic gastritis/duodenal ulcer confirms H. pylori-associated peptic ulcer disease; standard management is triple therapy — a PPI plus two antibiotics (commonly amoxicillin and clarithromycin, or metronidazole where resistance is a concern) for 14 days in children (ESPGHAN/NASPGHAN guideline) — achieving symptom resolution and eradication, reducing recurrence.

subject: Paediatrics
q: A 14-month-old girl brought for a routine visit is noted to have visible severe wasting with prominent ribs, no pedal edema, and a mid-upper arm circumference (MUAC) of 10.8 cm. Using WHO/IAP criteria, how should her nutritional status be classified?
why: Moderate acute malnutrition corresponds to a MUAC of 11.5-12.4cm, above this child's measured value.
A MUAC of 10.8cm is well below normal (≥12.5cm) and visible severe wasting confirms significant acute malnutrition, not a normal status.
This picture (visible wasting, low MUAC) reflects acute wasting, not merely chronic stunting, which is assessed separately using height-for-age.
Correct — MUAC <11.5cm meets the WHO/IAP criterion for severe acute malnutrition.
exp: WHO/IAP criteria define severe acute malnutrition in children 6-59 months by any one of: WHZ below -3 SD, MUAC <11.5cm, or bilateral pitting edema. A MUAC of 10.8cm alone is sufficient to classify SAM regardless of edema status, and mandates assessment for medical complications to decide inpatient versus outpatient management.

subject: Paediatrics
q: A 6-month-old infant presents with clusters of sudden flexor spasms of the neck, trunk, and limbs occurring in series, especially on waking. EEG shows a chaotic, high-amplitude, disorganized pattern (hypsarrhythmia). Examination reveals hypopigmented ash-leaf-shaped macules on the trunk. What is the most likely underlying diagnosis?
why: Neurofibromatosis type 1 presents with café-au-lait macules and neurofibromas, not ash-leaf hypopigmented macules or classic infantile spasms.
Correct — ash-leaf macules plus infantile spasms/hypsarrhythmia is the classic early presentation of tuberous sclerosis complex.
Sturge-Weber syndrome presents with a facial port-wine stain in the trigeminal distribution and leptomeningeal angiomatosis, not ash-leaf macules.
Ataxia-telangiectasia presents later in childhood with progressive cerebellar ataxia and oculocutaneous telangiectasias, not infantile spasms in a 6-month-old.
exp: Infantile spasms (West syndrome) with hypsarrhythmia on EEG, associated with hypopigmented ash-leaf macules, points strongly to tuberous sclerosis complex — one of the most common identifiable causes of infantile spasms. Later cutaneous/systemic clues include facial angiofibromas, shagreen patches, subependymal giant cell astrocytomas, and cardiac rhabdomyomas; vigabatrin is particularly effective here.

subject: Paediatrics
q: An 8-month-old infant has cough, a respiratory rate of 58/min, and lower chest wall indrawing, but is alert, feeding well, with no cyanosis or other danger signs. As per IMNCI classification, this infant has:
why: No pneumonia has neither fast breathing nor indrawing
Pneumonia (fast breathing alone) does not include chest indrawing
Correct - IMNCI classifies chest indrawing, even without general danger signs, as severe pneumonia
Very severe disease needs an additional general danger sign, absent here
exp: IMNCI (India's adaptation of the WHO ARI programme) classifies chest indrawing - even without general danger signs - as severe pneumonia needing urgent referral with a pre-referral antibiotic dose; fast breathing alone is pneumonia (home antibiotics), and an added danger sign upgrades to very severe disease. Note: WHO's 2014 revised global guideline treats isolated indrawing without danger signs as simple pneumonia - India's IMNCI teaching still uses the severe-pneumonia classification, which NEET PG questions typically follow.

subject: Paediatrics
q: A 2-year-old boy has failure to thrive, polyuria, and hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis with a normal anion gap. Urine pH remains persistently above 5.5 despite systemic acidosis, and serum potassium is low. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why: Proximal RTA is due to defective bicarbonate reabsorption; urine pH can fall below 5.5 once the reduced reabsorptive threshold is exceeded
Type 4 RTA is associated with hyperkalemia, not hypokalemia
Correct - distal RTA cannot acidify urine below 5.5 despite systemic acidosis, with hypokalemia and nephrocalcinosis risk
DKA shows hyperglycemia, ketonuria, and an elevated anion gap, not a normal-anion-gap picture
exp: Distal (type 1) RTA results from impaired H+ secretion by alpha-intercalated cells of the collecting duct, so urine cannot be acidified below pH 5.5 even during systemic acidosis; associated hypokalemia and risk of nephrocalcinosis/nephrolithiasis distinguish it from proximal RTA.

subject: Paediatrics
q: A 4-year-old unimmunized child presents with sudden high-grade fever, a muffled voice, and preference to sit leaning forward (tripod positioning). Which feature best distinguishes this from viral croup?
opts: Abrupt onset with toxic appearance and drooling
why: Barking cough is characteristic of croup, not epiglottitis
Stridor can occur in both conditions, so it does not discriminate
Epiglottitis causes high, not low, fever
Correct - abrupt onset over hours with toxicity and drooling marks epiglottitis
exp: Acute epiglottitis (classically H. influenzae type b in unimmunized children) has an abrupt onset over hours with high fever, toxic look, and drooling, unlike croup's gradual 1-2 day evolution with a barking cough.

subject: Paediatrics
q: A 3-week-old neonate presents with progressive constipation, abdominal distension, and explosive stool release on digital rectal examination. Which historical feature most strongly suggests Hirschsprung disease over functional constipation?
opts: Good response to increased fiber and fluids
Onset since birth with delayed meconium passage
why: Onset after starting solids favors functional constipation
Encopresis/soiling is typical of functional constipation
Good response to conservative fiber/fluid measures argues against Hirschsprung, which needs surgical resection
Correct - onset from birth with delayed meconium reflects congenital aganglionosis
exp: Hirschsprung disease presents from birth with delayed meconium passage beyond 48 hours, progressive abdominal distension, and explosive stool on DRE, reflecting congenital aganglionosis causing functional obstruction.

subject: Paediatrics
q: A 2-month-old infant born to consanguineous parents presents with massive proteinuria, generalized edema, and a large placenta noted at birth, with progressive renal failure. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Congenital nephrotic syndrome of the Finnish type
why: Minimal change disease typically presents later (2-6 years) and is steroid-responsive, with no placental enlargement
PSGN presents later in childhood post-infection with hematuria/hypertension
HSP nephritis presents with the characteristic purpuric rash and arthritis in older children, not neonates
Correct - NPHS1/nephrin mutation, consanguinity risk, presents in first 3 months with enlarged placenta
exp: Congenital nephrotic syndrome, Finnish type (NPHS1/nephrin gene mutation, autosomal recessive) presents within the first 3 months of life with massive proteinuria, edema, and an enlarged placenta, progressing to ESRD.

subject: Paediatrics
q: A 6-month-old girl presents with her second episode of culture-proven febrile urinary tract infection. After the acute infection resolves, which imaging investigation is most appropriate to look for an underlying anatomical cause?
opts: Ultrasound of the kidneys/bladder plus a micturating cystourethrogram (MCUG) to assess for vesicoureteric reflux
why: DMSA detects renal scarring/acute pyelonephritis but not anatomy/reflux
Doppler assesses vascular flow, not reflux/anatomy
IVU is outdated for this indication
Correct
exp: A recurrent febrile UTI in an infant warrants a renal-bladder ultrasound plus an MCUG to grade vesicoureteric reflux (VUR), the commonest underlying anomaly predisposing to recurrent pyelonephritis and renal scarring in young children.

subject: Paediatrics
q: A 7-year-old with diabetic ketoacidosis is started on an IV insulin infusion after an initial fluid bolus. His admission potassium was 4.2 mEq/L and he has just passed urine. What is the correct next step regarding potassium?
opts: Withhold all potassium until the insulin infusion is stopped
Give a rapid IV potassium bolus before starting insulin
Add potassium only if the child becomes symptomatic with arrhythmia
Add potassium to the IV fluids now, since insulin will drive potassium intracellularly and urine output confirms adequate renal function
why: Withholding risks dangerous hypokalemia once insulin therapy begins
Potassium is never given as a rapid IV bolus (risk of fatal arrhythmia)
Waiting for symptoms means acting too late, since hypokalemia can cause silent fatal arrhythmias
Correct
exp: In paediatric DKA, insulin shifts potassium intracellularly and can precipitate life-threatening hypokalemia even with a normal admission level; once urine output and a non-elevated K+ are confirmed, potassium should be added to fluids alongside or just before starting insulin, never as a bolus.

subject: Paediatrics
q: A term newborn develops visible jaundice within the first 24 hours of life; total serum bilirubin is markedly elevated with a rapidly rising rate. What is the most important next step in evaluation?
opts: Reassure as physiological jaundice and repeat bilirubin at 72 hours
Send maternal and infant blood group, direct Coombs test, and reticulocyte count to evaluate for hemolytic disease
Start phototherapy without further workup and discharge
Advise switching from breastfeeding to formula
why: Jaundice in the first 24h is never labelled physiological, so reassurance alone is wrong
Correct — hemolysis workup (blood group, Coombs, reticulocyte count) is mandatory given the timing
Phototherapy may follow the bilirubin nomogram but the underlying cause must still be sought
Breastfeeding jaundice presents later (day 3-5) and is a diagnosis of exclusion, not the concern here
exp: Jaundice appearing within the first 24 hours of life is always pathological (never physiological) and mandates urgent evaluation for hemolytic disease — maternal/infant blood grouping, direct Coombs test, and reticulocyte count — because ABO/Rh incompatibility carries the highest risk of rapid bilirubin rise and kernicterus. Physiological jaundice appears after 24h, peaks day 3-5 (term), and resolves by day 7-10.

subject: Paediatrics
q: A 4-year-old boy presents with periorbital puffiness, frothy urine, and generalized edema with heavy proteinuria and a bland sediment. Empirical oral steroids achieve complete remission within 2 weeks. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why: Membranous nephropathy is rare in young children and typically steroid-resistant
Correct — MCD is the most common childhood nephrotic cause and classically steroid-responsive
FSGS is a steroid-resistant cause of childhood nephrotic syndrome
MPGN presents with a nephritic-nephrotic picture (low complement, hematuria), generally steroid-resistant
exp: Minimal change disease is the most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in children (1-8 years), characteristically steroid-responsive (remission within 2-4 weeks in over 90%), which is why empirical steroid therapy without biopsy is standard first-line management, reserving biopsy for atypical or steroid-resistant cases.

subject: Paediatrics
q: A preterm infant born at 30 weeks develops grunting, nasal flaring, and retractions with cyanosis within hours of birth; CXR shows a diffuse reticulogranular ground-glass pattern with air bronchograms. What is the underlying defect?
opts: Delayed clearance of fetal lung fluid
Persistent pulmonary hypertension with right-to-left shunting
why: Delayed fluid clearance describes transient tachypnea of the newborn, with perihilar streaking resolving in 24-72h
Meconium aspiration shows patchy infiltrates/hyperinflation, typically term/post-term
PPHN is often a secondary complication rather than the primary defect here
Correct — surfactant deficiency causes the classic RDS ground-glass pattern
exp: Respiratory Distress Syndrome (Hyaline Membrane Disease) results from developmental surfactant deficiency in preterm lungs, causing alveolar collapse (increased surface tension), reduced compliance, and the classic ground-glass/air-bronchogram appearance; antenatal corticosteroids (24-34 weeks) and postnatal surfactant replacement are the mainstays of prevention/treatment.

subject: Paediatrics
q: An 18-month-old, thriving child with normal growth passes 4-5 loose stools daily containing undigested vegetable particles, worse with excess fruit juice intake, with no blood, fever, or weight loss. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Chronic non-specific diarrhoea of childhood (toddler's diarrhea)
why: Celiac disease typically causes malabsorption with growth faltering, not seen here
Giardiasis usually has more malabsorptive features and needs stool testing to diagnose
CF causes poor growth and respiratory symptoms, not an isolated well-thriving diarrhea picture
Correct - a functional diagnosis in a well-thriving toddler with these classic triggers
exp: Toddler's diarrhea (chronic nonspecific diarrhea of childhood) is a functional diagnosis in a thriving 1-3 year-old passing frequent loose stools with visible undigested food, often provoked by excessive fruit juice/sorbitol and low dietary fat - reassurance and dietary modification is the management, provided red flags like growth faltering, blood, or nocturnal symptoms are absent.

subject: Paediatrics
q: A 6-year-old boy develops periorbital puffiness, smoky-colored urine, and blood pressure of 130/90 mmHg two weeks after a sore throat, with mild proteinuria on urinalysis. Which feature best distinguishes this presentation from nephrotic syndrome?
opts: Hematuria and hypertension with only mild proteinuria
why: Edema occurs in both nephritic and nephrotic presentations, not discriminating
Hypoalbuminemia this low is a nephrotic feature, not typical of isolated post-streptococcal AGN
Nephrotic-range proteinuria defines nephrotic syndrome, not this nephritic presentation
Correct - the classic nephritic picture of post-streptococcal AGN
exp: Post-streptococcal AGN classically presents with the nephritic picture of hematuria, hypertension, and only mild-to-moderate proteinuria (latency ~2 weeks post-pharyngitis, transiently low C3), unlike nephrotic syndrome's massive proteinuria and hypoalbuminemia with generalized edema.

subject: Paediatrics
q: A 7-year-old girl presents with breast budding (Tanner stage 2) and a recent growth spurt, with no other pubertal signs and a normal neurological examination. What is the appropriate definition-based next step in evaluation?
opts: Reassure - this is normal puberty timing for girls
Confirm with a bone age radiograph plus basal LH, FSH and estradiol as the initial workup
Start a GnRH analogue immediately, before any investigation
No workup needed unless menarche occurs
why: Breast development before age 8 is, by definition, precocious and warrants evaluation, not reassurance
Correct - bone age plus basal gonadotropins/estradiol is the appropriate initial workup
Starting treatment before establishing a central cause is wrong - a peripheral cause will not respond to a GnRH analogue
Waiting for menarche misses the window for early evaluation and intervention
exp: Precocious puberty in girls is defined as onset of secondary sexual characteristics before age 8. Bone age plus basal (ultrasensitive) LH and estradiol is the standard first-step workup; a GnRH agonist stimulation test is reserved for when basal LH is indeterminate, to distinguish central from peripheral precocious puberty before starting treatment.

subject: Paediatrics
q: An 8-month-old infant has the first episode of wheeze, low-grade fever, and rhinorrhea for 2 days, with fine crackles and prolonged expiration on auscultation, feeding adequately. What is the most appropriate initial management approach?
opts: Supportive care - hydration, nasal suctioning, and monitoring
Empirical antibiotics for likely bacterial pneumonia
why: Bronchodilators have not shown consistent benefit in bronchiolitis, unlike asthma
Correct - the mainstay of management for bronchiolitis; bronchodilators, steroids and antibiotics have not shown consistent benefit
Systemic corticosteroids have not shown benefit in bronchiolitis
Bronchiolitis is viral; antibiotics aren't indicated without evidence of bacterial superinfection
exp: Bronchiolitis (classically RSV, first episode of wheeze in an infant with a preceding viral prodrome) is managed supportively - hydration, nasal suctioning, oxygen if hypoxic - since bronchodilators, corticosteroids, and antibiotics have not shown consistent benefit in trials, unlike the bronchodilator/steroid-responsive picture of asthma in recurrent wheeze in older children.

subject: Paediatrics
q: A 6-year-old presents with fever, sore throat, a diffuse sandpaper-like rash that spares the palms and soles, a strawberry tongue, and flushed cheeks with circumoral pallor. The most likely diagnosis is:
why: Measles produces a cephalocaudal maculopapular rash with Koplik spots and the 3 C's, a different pattern
Kawasaki disease shows a polymorphous rash with conjunctival injection and extremity changes, lacking sandpaper texture
Correct — classic scarlet fever presentation
Roseola infantum shows a rash appearing after fever resolves, in infants, unlike this concurrent febrile illness
exp: Scarlet fever is caused by erythrogenic exotoxin-producing group A Streptococcus, producing a diffuse fine sandpaper rash sparing the palms/soles/circumoral area, a strawberry tongue, and Pastia's lines; treatment is penicillin to reduce the risk of rheumatic fever and other complications.

subject: Paediatrics
q: A 4-month-old presents with 2 days of coryza followed by tachypnoea, audible wheeze, and fine bilateral crepitations, with mild subcostal retractions but adequate oxygen saturation on room air. The most likely diagnosis and its typical causative agent is:
why: Bacterial pneumonia more typically shows focal crepitations/consolidation and a toxic-looking child, without this coryzal-then-wheeze pattern
C. trachomatis pneumonia is typically afebrile with a staccato cough and tachypnoea without wheeze, often with conjunctivitis in the first 3 months of life
Croup causes a barking cough and inspiratory stridor from upper airway involvement, not lower-airway wheeze/crepitations
Correct — classic bronchiolitis presentation and aetiology
exp: Bronchiolitis is the commonest lower respiratory tract infection in infants under 2 years, most frequently caused by RSV, presenting with a coryzal prodrome followed by tachypnoea, wheeze, and crepitations from small airway inflammation; management is primarily supportive.

subject: Paediatrics
q: A term neonate fails to pass meconium within 48 hours of birth, with progressive abdominal distension; abdominal X-ray shows a soap bubble (ground-glass) appearance of bowel loops in the right lower quadrant without significant air-fluid levels, and a Gastrografin contrast enema is planned as both diagnostic and potentially therapeutic. This presentation should prompt screening for:
why: Hirschsprung disease is a differential for neonatal obstruction, but the enema shows a rectosigmoid transition zone (not this soap-bubble sign), and diagnosis is by rectal suction biopsy
Correct — meconium ileus is essentially a marker for underlying cystic fibrosis
Congenital hypothyroidism can cause severe constipation but not this contrast-enema-treatable inspissated meconium pattern
NEC typically presents later, in preterm neonates with feeding intolerance and pneumatosis intestinalis, a different process
exp: Meconium ileus — obstruction of the distal ileum by abnormally thick, tenacious meconium producing the soap-bubble sign — is caused in the vast majority of cases by cystic fibrosis due to CFTR-mediated abnormal chloride/water transport making secretions viscid; every affected neonate should be worked up for cystic fibrosis.

subject: Paediatrics
q: A term neonate on day 2 of life shows repetitive lip-smacking, bicycling limb movements, and eye deviation that cannot be stopped by holding the limb still. Video-EEG confirms an electrographic correlate. What is this most consistent with?
why: Jitteriness is stimulus-sensitive and stops with passive holding, with no eye deviation
Sleep myoclonus occurs only in sleep and stops on waking, with no EEG correlate
Correct, subtle seizures are not suppressed by restraint and are confirmed by EEG correlate
Hyperekplexia is an exaggerated startle response to stimuli, not this pattern
exp: The key bedside discriminator between neonatal jitteriness and seizure is that jitteriness stops when the limb is passively held/flexed, whereas true seizure activity continues despite restraint. Subtle seizures (oculomotor, oral-buccal, or bicycling movements) are the commonest neonatal seizure semiology and are easily missed without EEG.

subject: Paediatrics
q: A 13-year-old boy being evaluated for short stature has a predicted adult height significantly below target height. His hand-wrist X-ray is compared against a standard reference atlas to estimate skeletal maturity. Which method is being used?
why: Tanner staging assesses pubertal/secondary sexual characteristics, not radiographic bone maturity
Ballard scoring assesses gestational age in newborns, not applicable at 13 years
Correct, compares a hand-wrist radiograph against a standard atlas to estimate skeletal age
Denver screening assesses developmental milestones in young children, unrelated
exp: Bone age lagging behind chronological age by more than 2 years suggests constitutional delay or a growth-suppressing condition (hypothyroidism, GH deficiency), while advanced bone age suggests precocious puberty or another cause of accelerated maturation - a core discriminator in the short-stature workup.

subject: Paediatrics
q: A 5-week-old first-born male infant presents with progressively worsening non-bilious projectile vomiting after feeds, visible peristalsis, and a palpable olive mass in the right upper quadrant. Venous blood gas shows pH 7.52, low chloride, and low potassium. What is the expected acid-base/electrolyte pattern?
opts: Anion gap metabolic acidosis with hyperkalemia
why: This pattern is more typical of renal tubular acidosis, not pyloric stenosis
The primary disturbance here is metabolic, not respiratory, and electrolytes are clearly deranged
An anion gap acidosis with hyperkalemia would suggest DKA or renal failure, not pyloric stenosis
Correct, repeated vomiting of HCl-rich gastric contents causes loss of H+ and Cl-, with renal compensation driving hypokalemia
exp: Correcting the fluid, chloride, and potassium deficits with normal saline plus KCl BEFORE pyloromyotomy is essential - operating on a metabolically alkalotic infant risks post-operative apnea from the alkalosis suppressing respiratory drive; surgery is elective, not emergent, precisely to allow this correction first.

subject: Paediatrics
q: A 7-month-old girl is brought to the outpatient clinic because her weight gain has stalled, having crossed two major percentile lines downward on the WHO growth chart over the past 3 months while exclusively breastfed with delayed and erratic complementary feeding. Examination reveals no dysmorphic features and a normal systemic exam, but the history uncovers a mother who appears withdrawn and overwhelmed. What is the most likely category of failure to thrive?
opts: Organic FTT due to congenital heart disease
Non-organic (psychosocial) FTT due to inadequate caloric intake
Organic FTT due to celiac disease
Normal growth variant, no intervention needed
why: No cardiac signs/symptoms are described, and normal systemic exam argues against occult cardiac disease
Correct, normal exam plus clear psychosocial/feeding-inadequacy history points to non-organic FTT
Celiac disease typically presents with GI symptoms not described here
Crossing two major percentile lines is significant growth faltering requiring intervention, not observation
exp: Roughly 80 percent of failure to thrive cases are non-organic/psychosocial in origin (inadequate caloric intake from feeding practices, poverty, or maternal depression/anxiety) rather than an underlying organic disease - a thorough dietary and psychosocial history is more cost-effective than an extensive organic workup when exam is normal.

subject: Paediatrics
q: A term neonate born to a mother with no documented antenatal group B Streptococcus (GBS) screening and prolonged rupture of membranes (over 18 hours) develops respiratory distress, temperature instability, and lethargy within the first 24 hours of life. Blood culture grows GBS. Which intrapartum measure, had it been given, would most effectively have reduced this risk?
opts: Intrapartum intravenous penicillin/ampicillin prophylaxis to the mother
Postnatal vitamin K to the neonate
Early initiation of breastfeeding within 1 hour of birth
why: Antenatal corticosteroids reduce RDS/IVH risk from prematurity, not GBS sepsis risk
Correct, intrapartum IV penicillin G or ampicillin started at least 4 hours before delivery reduces early-onset GBS disease
Vitamin K prevents hemorrhagic disease of the newborn, unrelated to sepsis
Early breastfeeding has general benefits but does not specifically prevent early-onset GBS sepsis
exp: Early-onset GBS disease (within 7 days, usually first 24-48h) is transmitted vertically during labor/delivery from a colonized maternal genital tract; universal antenatal GBS screening at 35-37 weeks (where feasible) or a risk-factor-based approach triggers intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis, the single most effective preventive intervention. Universal antenatal GBS culture screening is not yet standard practice everywhere in India; risk-factor-based prophylaxis is more commonly used.

subject: Paediatrics
q: A 2-year-old child ingests a button battery which lodges in the mid-esophagus, confirmed on X-ray by a halo/double-ring sign. What is the most urgent next step in management?
opts: Observe with serial X-rays, expecting spontaneous passage
Induce vomiting with syrup of ipecac to expel the object
Administer a PEG-based bowel preparation and await passage
why: Wrong — observation is appropriate for coins, not batteries; delay risks perforation/fistula.
Wrong — inducing emesis risks aspiration and does not address the causticity of a lodged battery; contraindicated.
Wrong — bowel prep applies to objects that have already passed the pylorus, not an esophageal battery.
Correct — button batteries in the esophagus need removal within 2 hours regardless of symptoms.
exp: A button battery lodged in the esophagus is a true paediatric emergency — it generates hydroxide ions at its negative pole via an external current, causing rapid liquefactive necrosis; perforation, fistula, or stricture can occur within 2 hours regardless of symptoms. This mandates emergent endoscopic removal, unlike coins which can often be observed for 12-24 hours if asymptomatic.

subject: Paediatrics
q: A 1-year-old with acute watery diarrhoea and some dehydration is being managed at home with WHO low-osmolarity ORS. What is the sodium concentration (mmol/L) of this current formulation?
why: Correct — the current low-osmolarity WHO-ORS standard has Na+ 75 mmol/L.
Wrong — 90 mmol/L was the older, pre-2002 standard-osmolarity ORS sodium content, now superseded.
Wrong — 111 mmol/L is not a standard ORS sodium value.
Wrong — 50 mmol/L underestimates the formulation's actual sodium content.
exp: The WHO low-osmolarity ORS (2002 revision) contains Na+ 75 mmol/L, glucose 75 mmol/L, K+ 20 mmol/L, citrate 10 mmol/L, total osmolarity 245 mOsm/L. Compared to the older standard-osmolarity ORS (Na+ 90 mmol/L), it reduces stool output, vomiting, and the need for supplemental IV fluids.

subject: Paediatrics
q: A previously healthy 22-kg, 6-year-old child is admitted for elective surgery and requires maintenance intravenous fluids calculated using the Holliday-Segar formula. What is his hourly maintenance fluid rate?
why: Correct — applying the 4-2-1 rule to 22 kg gives 62 ml per hour.
52 ml per hour reflects an arithmetic underestimate of the last increment.
72 ml per hour overestimates the requirement beyond the standard formula for 22 kg.
42 ml per hour corresponds to a child of about 10 to 12 kg, an underestimate for 22 kg.
exp: The Holliday-Segar 4-2-1 formula gives maintenance fluid as 4 ml/kg/hr for the first 10 kg, 2 ml/kg/hr for the next 10 kg, and 1 ml/kg/hr for each kg above 20 kg. For 22 kg: 40 plus 20 plus 2 equals 62 ml/hr. Current IAP/NNF practice favours isotonic fluids rather than hypotonic maintenance fluids in hospitalised children, given the risk of hospital-acquired hyponatraemia.

subject: Paediatrics
q: A 5-year-old unimmunized child presents with fever and sore throat, and examination shows a thick, adherent grayish-white membrane over the tonsils and posterior pharynx that bleeds when a swab attempts to remove it, along with marked cervical lymphadenopathy causing a swollen bull neck. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why: Infectious mononucleosis causes exudative tonsillitis and lymphadenopathy but not an adherent, bleeding pseudomembrane
Streptococcal pharyngitis gives a patchy exudate that wipes off easily, unlike diphtheria's adherent bleeding membrane
Peritonsillar abscess causes trismus and uvular deviation without a membrane
Correct — an unimmunized child with a bleeding adherent pseudomembrane and bull neck is diphtheria until proven otherwise
exp: Corynebacterium diphtheriae exotoxin causes coagulative necrosis of the pharyngeal mucosa, forming a tough, adherent grey pseudomembrane that bleeds on attempted removal; cervical lymphadenitis with soft-tissue edema produces the classic bull neck, and the same toxin can cause myocarditis and a delayed demyelinating polyneuropathy if antitoxin is not given promptly.

subject: Paediatrics
q: A 6-year-old boy develops a palpable purpuric rash over the buttocks and extensor surfaces of both legs, colicky abdominal pain, and arthralgia of the knees and ankles, followed a few days later by hematuria and proteinuria. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why: PSGN follows streptococcal infection with an isolated nephritic picture, not palpable purpura, arthralgia, and abdominal pain
Correct — purpura plus arthralgia plus abdominal pain plus nephritis is the classic HSP/IgA vasculitis tetrad
HUS follows bloody diarrhoea with microangiopathic hemolytic anemia and thrombocytopenia, not a purpuric rash with arthralgia
Minimal change disease presents with nephrotic-range proteinuria and edema, not purpura or preceding joint/GI symptoms
exp: IgA vasculitis (Henoch-Schonlein purpura) is the commonest vasculitis of childhood, presenting with the tetrad of palpable purpura over dependent/extensor areas, arthralgia, colicky abdominal pain, and nephritis from mesangial IgA deposition — the same underlying pathophysiology as IgA nephropathy — so renal function and urinalysis must be monitored even after the rash resolves.

subject: Paediatrics
q: A 9-year-old child with newly diagnosed diabetic ketoacidosis is started on isotonic fluid resuscitation and an insulin infusion. Four hours later she develops headache, bradycardia, and a falling Glasgow Coma Scale score. What is the most appropriate immediate step?
opts: Give a rapid additional 20 mL/kg normal saline bolus
Give IV mannitol or hypertonic (3%) saline and slow the fluid rate
Increase the insulin infusion rate to correct hyperglycemia faster
Start empirical antibiotics for suspected sepsis
why: A further rapid fluid bolus risks worsening the cerebral edema that is likely developing, rather than treating it.
Correct — headache, bradycardia, and falling GCS in a child on DKA treatment are warning signs of cerebral edema, requiring emergency hyperosmolar therapy and a slower fluid rate.
Accelerating insulin causes a faster fall in glucose/osmolality, a recognized risk factor for precipitating or worsening cerebral edema.
Antibiotics do not address the acute neurological deterioration and should not delay emergency treatment of suspected cerebral edema.
exp: Cerebral edema is the most feared complication of paediatric DKA treatment, typically emerging 4-12 hours after starting therapy. Warning signs are headache, bradycardia, and declining consciousness/GCS — treat immediately with mannitol or 3% hypertonic saline and slow the fluid infusion rate. Overly rapid fluid or osmolar correction is a recognized risk factor, which is why current protocols favour more gradual rehydration than older regimens. Exact mannitol/hypertonic saline doses vary slightly between protocols (ISPAD).

subject: Paediatrics
q: A 4-year-old boy with known steroid-sensitive nephrotic syndrome, currently relapsing with generalized edema, develops fever, abdominal pain, and abdominal guarding. Ascitic fluid tap shows neutrophilic pleocytosis. What is the most likely diagnosis and organism?
opts: Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis due to Streptococcus pneumoniae
Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis due to Escherichia coli
why: Correct — the classic organism in nephrotic-syndrome-associated SBP, driven by urinary immunoglobulin/factor B loss.
Appendicitis does not explain the nephrotic relapse or the diffuse ascitic neutrophilia, and usually gives localized right iliac fossa signs.
E. coli is the typical organism in cirrhotic-ascites SBP, not nephrotic-syndrome-associated peritonitis.
Tuberculous peritonitis is a more chronic, indolent process, not this acute presentation.
exp: Children with nephrotic syndrome relapse are predisposed to spontaneous bacterial peritonitis, classically due to Streptococcus pneumoniae, because urinary loss of IgG and complement factor B (alternate/properdin pathway) impairs opsonization of encapsulated organisms.

subject: Paediatrics
q: An 8-month-old infant with 3 days of watery diarrhoea is lethargic, has sunken eyes, and drinks poorly. The skin pinch goes back very slowly (more than 2 seconds) and the radial pulse is feeble - severe dehydration. As per WHO/IMNCI Plan C for an infant under 12 months, the initial IV fluid regimen (Ringer lactate) is:
opts: Maintenance-rate normal saline only, reassess in 6 hours
30 ml/kg over the first 30 minutes, then 70 ml/kg over the next 2.5 hours
30 ml/kg over the first 1 hour, then 70 ml/kg over the next 5 hours
why: That volume/route is Plan B (some dehydration, oral ORS), not IV Plan C for severe dehydration
Maintenance-only fluids under-resuscitate a child in hypovolaemic shock and delay correction
This is the correct timing for a child 12 months or older, not for this 8-month-old infant
Correct — this is the infant-specific Plan C schedule
exp: WHO Plan C for severe dehydration splits by age: infants under 12 months get 30 ml/kg IV Ringer lactate over the first 1 hour followed by 70 ml/kg over the next 5 hours (total 6 hours); children 12 months and older get the same volumes compressed into 30 minutes then 2.5 hours (total 3 hours). Using the older child's faster schedule in a young infant risks fluid overload.

subject: Paediatrics
q: A 10-year-old boy has recurrent episodes of gross and microscopic hematuria. His maternal uncle and grandfather both developed progressive renal failure in their 20s-30s. On examination he has bilateral sensorineural hearing loss, and slit-lamp exam shows anterior lenticonus. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why: Correct — hematuria plus sensorineural deafness plus anterior lenticonus with an X-linked family pattern is classic Alport syndrome
PSGN follows streptococcal infection by 1-2 weeks, with no deafness or eye findings, and is usually self-limited
IgA nephropathy causes synpharyngitic hematuria but no hearing loss, lenticonus, or X-linked male pattern
Minimal change disease presents as nephrotic syndrome, not primarily hematuria, with no extrarenal features
exp: Alport syndrome (X-linked COL4A5 mutation in most families) presents with progressive hematuric nephritis, sensorineural hearing loss, and ocular findings such as anterior lenticonus; affected male maternal relatives with renal failure reflect the X-linked inheritance pattern.

subject: Paediatrics
q: An 8-month-old infant with acute gastroenteritis and reduced feeding presents with lethargy, doughy skin turgor, and serum sodium of 168 mEq/L. What is the recommended maximum safe rate of fall of serum sodium during rehydration?
why: 2 mEq/L/hr is too rapid and risks cerebral edema
Correct — the accepted safe ceiling
5 mEq/L/hr is grossly excessive
Full correction within 6 hours is dangerously fast and contraindicated in hypernatremic dehydration
exp: In hypernatremic dehydration, serum sodium should be lowered no faster than about 0.5 mEq/L/hour (roughly 10 to 12 mEq/L over 24 hours), rehydrating over 48 hours, because too-rapid correction drops plasma osmolality faster than brain cells can adjust, causing cerebral edema and seizures.

subject: Paediatrics
q: A 28-week preterm neonate, previously tolerating feeds, develops abdominal distension, bilious aspirates, and blood-streaked stools on day 10 of life. Image described: abdominal X-ray shows pneumatosis intestinalis with no free air or portal venous gas. Which modified Bell stage of necrotizing enterocolitis best fits this presentation?
opts: Stage IIIA — advanced NEC, bowel intact
why: Stage I is suspected NEC with nonspecific signs and no pneumatosis on imaging, which does not match this X-ray
Stage IIB requires additional findings of portal venous gas plus acidosis or thrombocytopenia, absent here
Correct — pneumatosis intestinalis with clinical signs of NEC and no portal gas or free air defines Stage IIA, mild definite NEC
Stage IIIA denotes advanced disease with hypotension, severe acidosis, and DIC, not described here
exp: Modified Bell staging guides NEC management: Stage I (suspected) has nonspecific signs; Stage IIA (mild, definite NEC) adds pneumatosis intestinalis; Stage IIB (moderate) adds portal venous gas plus acidosis/thrombocytopenia; Stage III (advanced) has systemic shock with or without perforation. Pneumatosis intestinalis alone, without portal gas or systemic collapse, is the hallmark of Stage IIA.

subject: Paediatrics
q: A 4-month-old infant, immunized with only the birth dose of vaccines, presents with 2 weeks of paroxysmal coughing fits ending in an inspiratory whoop and post-tussive vomiting. Total leukocyte count is 32,000/mm3 with 80% lymphocytes. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why: Correct - paroxysmal whooping cough with post-tussive vomiting and marked lymphocytosis in an under-immunized infant is classic pertussis
Bronchiolitis (RSV) presents with wheeze and respiratory distress, not a 2-week paroxysmal whooping illness
Viral croup presents with a barking cough and stridor, not paroxysmal whoop
Foreign body aspiration has a sudden choking-onset history, not a progressive 2-week illness
exp: Classic pertussis has a catarrhal stage (most infectious), a paroxysmal stage (cough paroxysms with inspiratory whoop and post-tussive vomiting), and a convalescent stage. Absolute lymphocytosis is a characteristic lab finding caused by a Bordetella pertussis toxin that inhibits lymphocyte migration into tissues. Under-immunized infants (India's UIP gives DPT at 6, 10, 14 weeks) carry the highest risk of severe disease.

subject: Paediatrics
q: A 10-year-old boy has height at the 3rd percentile with delayed onset of puberty. His growth velocity is normal for age, bone age on left hand-wrist X-ray reads 8 years, and his father recalls being a similarly short late bloomer who caught up and grew normally as an adult. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Constitutional delay of growth and puberty (CDGP)
why: Correct - matches delayed bone age plus normal velocity plus positive family history of delayed but eventually normal puberty
Familial short stature has bone age concordant with chronological age and no pubertal delay
GH deficiency causes a subnormal growth velocity, which is preserved here
Hypothyroidism causes reduced growth velocity and other systemic signs, not an isolated constitutional pattern
exp: CDGP is characterised by bone age lagging behind chronological age (roughly matching height age), a preserved normal growth velocity, delayed puberty, and a positive family history of late bloomers who eventually reach normal adult height - a normal variant, not pathology, distinguished from familial short stature (bone age = chronological age) and from GH deficiency/hypothyroidism (subnormal growth velocity).

subject: Paediatrics
q: A previously healthy 3-week-old, exclusively breastfed neonate develops sudden onset of bilious vomiting with irritability and abdominal distension. Upper GI contrast study shows an abnormal corkscrew appearance of the proximal small bowel. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why: Pyloric stenosis causes non-bilious projectile vomiting, typically presenting at 3-6 weeks of age
Correct — the corkscrew sign on upper GI contrast study is specific for malrotation with midgut volvulus, a surgical emergency
NEC typically occurs in preterm infants with bloody stools and pneumatosis intestinalis on X-ray
Duodenal atresia gives a double-bubble sign and usually presents on day 1 of life, not a corkscrew pattern
exp: Bilious vomiting in a neonate is a surgical emergency until malrotation with midgut volvulus is excluded — delay risks midgut ischemia and short-gut syndrome. Upper GI contrast series is the gold-standard investigation, showing the corkscrew or bird's-beak sign of the twisted duodenum/proximal jejunum with an abnormally positioned duodenojejunal (ligament of Treitz) junction. Emergency Ladd's procedure is required.

subject: Paediatrics
q: A 3-year-old girl has poor weight gain, abdominal distension, irritability, and bulky foul-smelling stools for six months, with her growth curve crossing percentiles downward; serology shows a strongly positive anti-tissue transglutaminase IgA. What is the best next confirmatory step before starting a gluten-free diet?
opts: Duodenal biopsy performed while she is still on a gluten-containing diet
Empirical gluten-free diet trial without biopsy
why: Correct — duodenal biopsy showing villous atrophy, crypt hyperplasia, and intraepithelial lymphocytosis (Marsh grading), done while still consuming gluten, is the confirmatory step.
An empirical gluten-free trial before biopsy risks obscuring histology if the diagnosis is ever questioned later.
Stool reducing substances screens for carbohydrate malabsorption, not celiac disease specifically.
Sweat chloride testing is for cystic fibrosis, not indicated by this serology pattern.
exp: Celiac disease workup: strongly positive anti-tTG IgA (with total IgA to exclude deficiency) is followed by duodenal biopsy while the child remains on a gluten-containing diet, since starting a gluten-free diet first can normalize both serology and histology and obscure the diagnosis. Biopsy shows villous atrophy, crypt hyperplasia, and increased intraepithelial lymphocytes, graded by the Marsh classification. Note: ESPGHAN 2020 allows a non-biopsy pathway only under strict criteria (anti-tTG over 10x ULN plus positive EMA plus symptoms); exam-standard teaching still expects biopsy confirmation.

subject: Paediatrics
q: A 10-year-old boy has a height of 118 cm, far below the third percentile; his father is 165 cm tall and his mother is 150 cm tall. Using the mid-parental height formula, what does his target height calculation suggest about the cause of his short stature?
opts: Target height approximately 150 cm; his height is appropriate for this target, no workup needed
Mid-parental height applies only to girls, so it cannot be used for this boy
Target height approximately 164 cm; his height is within the normal target range, consistent with familial short stature
Target height approximately 164 cm; his height is far below the target range, favoring a pathological cause requiring workup
why: 150 cm is simply the mother's height, not the calculated mid-parental target.
The formula applies to both sexes with sex-specific adjustments (plus 13 cm for boys, minus 13 cm for girls before halving).
The approximately 164 cm target is correctly calculated, but 118 cm is far outside the expected range around it, so this is not consistent with familial short stature.
Correct — the large gap between actual and target height favors pathological short stature needing bone age and endocrine evaluation.
exp: Mid-parental height for a boy = (father's height + mother's height + 13)/2 = (165+150+13)/2, approximately 164 cm. His actual height of 118 cm is roughly 46 cm below this target, far outside the expected genetic range, pointing away from familial short stature toward a pathological cause. Note: the exact width conventionally cited for the expected target range (roughly plus/minus 8.5 to 10 cm, about 2 SD) varies by source; the plus-13/minus-13 calculation method itself is standard.

subject: Paediatrics
q: A 3-year-old boy is brought to OPD because his mother noticed pallor. He is thriving on a mixed family diet, with no pica and no bleeding; the spleen tip is just palpable. Hb 9.2 g/dL, MCV 62 fL, RBC count 5.4 million/cumm, RDW 13.1%, serum ferritin 48 ng/mL, transferrin saturation 28%. Smear shows microcytes and target cells with no basophilic stippling. Which is the most appropriate next investigation?
opts: Therapeutic trial of oral elemental iron 3 mg/kg/day for 4 weeks, then repeat haemoglobin
High-performance liquid chromatography for HbA2 quantification
Bone marrow aspiration with Perls stain
why: An iron trial is justified only when iron deficiency is plausible; ferritin 48 and TSAT 28% are both normal, so iron would only load an iron-replete child and waste a month

Correct: Mentzer index = 62/5.4 = 11.5 (below 13), with a HIGH RBC count despite anaemia, normal RDW and normal iron stores - the profile of beta-thalassaemia trait, confirmed by HbA2 of 3.5-7% on HPLC
Marrow adds nothing when peripheral blood plus HPLC answers the question; reserve it for sideroblastic anaemia or unexplained dysplasia
Lead poisoning is the other microcytic mimic but gives basophilic stippling, a normal-to-low RBC count and an exposure history, none present here
exp: In microcytic anaemia, read the Mentzer index (MCV divided by RBC count in millions) together with iron studies before treating. Mentzer below 13 with a HIGH RBC count, normal RDW and normal ferritin/TSAT means thalassaemia trait - go straight to HPLC for HbA2, not an iron trial. Mentzer above 13 with low ferritin means iron deficiency. Trap to remember: coexistent iron deficiency lowers HbA2 and can produce a false-negative carrier screen, so correct iron first and repeat HPLC.

subject: Paediatrics
q: A 5-week-old, term, appropriate-for-gestational-age neonate who passed normal yellow stools until 2 weeks of age now presents with persistently pale, clay-colored stools, dark urine, and worsening jaundice. Total bilirubin is elevated with a conjugated fraction of 60%. Which ultrasonographic finding would most strongly support the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Triangular cord sign at the porta hepatis
Gallbladder wall thickening with pericholecystic fluid
exp: Conjugated hyperbilirubinemia beyond 2 weeks of age with acholic stools should always raise suspicion for extrahepatic biliary atresia. The ultrasound triangular cord sign (an echogenic fibrous cord at the porta hepatis) is a classic non-invasive pointer; diagnosis is confirmed by hepatobiliary scintigraphy and intraoperative cholangiogram or liver biopsy. Kasai portoenterostomy done before 60 days of life gives the best outcome.

subject: Paediatrics
q: A 3-year-old develops bloody diarrhea, and five days later presents with pallor, oliguria, and petechiae; labs show anemia with schistocytes, thrombocytopenia, and elevated creatinine. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Disseminated intravascular coagulation due to sepsis
Hemolytic uremic syndrome due to Shiga-toxin producing E. coli
exp: The classic triad of microangiopathic hemolytic anemia (schistocytes), thrombocytopenia, and acute kidney injury following bloody diarrhea defines typical (diarrhea-associated) HUS from Shiga-toxin producing E. coli (O157:H7). Management is supportive; antibiotics are generally avoided as bacterial lysis may increase toxin release and worsen HUS risk.

subject: Paediatrics
q: An 8-year-old boy has choreiform movements and a positive milkmaid's grip, 3 months after an untreated febrile illness. ASO titer is normal and there is no arthritis or carditis. Under the 2015 Jones criteria revision, what is required to diagnose acute rheumatic fever in this child?
opts: A repeat ASO or anti-DNase B titer must be positive
At least one additional minor criterion must be present
Nothing further - chorea alone is sufficient, without evidence of antecedent GAS infection or any other criterion
Arthritis must be documented within the same illness episode
exp: Chorea and indolent carditis are the two Jones manifestations that stand alone: either one is sufficient to diagnose ARF without a second criterion and without laboratory evidence of preceding streptococcal infection (2015 AHA Jones revision). This exists precisely because of chorea's long latency - by the time it appears the serology has usually normalised.

subject: Paediatrics
q: A child with chorea, asked to close his eyes and hold them shut, shows fine eyelid flickering instead of sustained closure. This finding shares its underlying mechanism with which other classical sign of the same condition?
exp: Motor impersistence - the inability to sustain a voluntary contraction - is the single mechanism behind eyelid flickering, the darting tongue, and the milkmaid's grip. Recognising them as one phenomenon rather than three separate eponyms is what the exam is testing.

subject: Paediatrics
q: Cardiovascular examination in a child with newly diagnosed Sydenham chorea is entirely normal. What is the most appropriate next step to assess for cardiac involvement?
opts: No further cardiac workup needed if auscultation is normal
Chest X-ray to look for cardiomegaly
Echocardiography, since subclinical valvulitis is common even with a normal exam
Cardiac MRI as the first-line test
exp: Subclinical carditis - echo-detectable valvulitis with no murmur - is common in isolated-chorea ARF, and its presence changes prophylaxis duration. Echocardiography is mandatory in every suspected ARF case regardless of auscultation (WHF 2012 echo criteria; 2015 Jones revision).

subject: Paediatrics
q: ASO titer in a child with clinically typical Sydenham chorea returns within the normal range. What is the correct interpretation?
opts: Acute rheumatic fever is excluded and an alternative diagnosis should be sought
The result is expected given the long latency to chorea onset, and does not exclude the diagnosis
The test was performed incorrectly and must be repeated immediately
A normal ASO confirms this is PANDAS rather than Sydenham chorea
exp: Chorea has the longest latency of any Jones manifestation (weeks to ~6 months), so ASO has usually fallen back to normal by the time it appears. A normal ASO never excludes ARF-related chorea; anti-DNase B stays elevated longer and is the more useful test this late.

subject: Paediatrics
q: An 8-year-old with Sydenham chorea has movements troublesome enough to interfere with feeding and school. Which is the drug of choice for symptomatic control?
exp: Nelson names phenobarbital the drug of choice for symptomatic chorea; if it fails, haloperidol or chlorpromazine is added. Drugs are only for movements troublesome enough to disturb feeding, school or sleep - most chorea self-limits over weeks to months, so the default is no drug at all. Levodopa and amantadine treat hypokinetic (parkinsonian) states and would worsen a hyperkinetic disorder; methylphenidate is a stimulant and equally wrong.

subject: Paediatrics
q: Echocardiography in a child with isolated Sydenham chorea shows no valvulitis or regurgitation. What duration of secondary antibiotic prophylaxis is appropriate?
opts: 5 years or until age 21, whichever is longer
exp: ARF without carditis: 5 years or until age 21, whichever is longer. Carditis without residual valve disease: 10 years or until age 21. Carditis with persistent valve disease: 10 years or until age 40 (often lifelong). The tiering is by carditis status, and chorea patients still need full prophylaxis.

subject: Paediatrics
q: Which single investigation is most important to send before labelling a school-age child's new-onset chorea as Sydenham chorea?
opts: Serum ceruloplasmin / slit-lamp exam for Kayser-Fleischer rings, to exclude Wilson disease
Throat swab culture, to confirm GAS infection
EEG, to exclude an absence seizure variant
exp: Wilson disease is the must-not-miss mimic in a child with new movement disorder: untreated it is progressive and fatal, treated it is manageable. Ceruloplasmin plus slit-lamp for KF rings is the screen. A throat swab this late is usually negative and would not change management anyway.

subject: Paediatrics
q: A 13-year-old girl presents with chorea, a malar rash and photosensitivity. Which diagnosis becomes more likely than Sydenham chorea?
exp: Chorea is a recognised neuropsychiatric manifestation of SLE (and of antiphospholipid syndrome). Malar rash plus photosensitivity in an adolescent girl shifts the diagnosis decisively; check ANA and antiphospholipid antibodies rather than treating as ARF.

subject: Paediatrics
q: A child with chorea is asked to squeeze the examiner's fingers and cannot sustain a steady grip - it alternately tightens and relaxes. What is this sign called?
exp: Milkmaid's (relapsing) grip. The pronator sign is arms pronating when held above the head; spooning is wrist flexion with finger hyperextension on outstretched arms. All three are bedside expressions of the same motor impersistence.

subject: Paediatrics
q: Sydenham chorea shows its highest incidence in which demographic group?
exp: Girls aged 5-15 years, with roughly a 2:1 female predominance - notable because ARF overall has no such strong sex skew. Chorea is rare before age 5 and after adolescence.

subject: Paediatrics
q: A 6-year-old presents with 1 day of colicky abdominal pain and vomiting, stable vitals, mild periumbilical/epigastric tenderness, normal counts, and CRP 16. Ultrasound confirms intussusception. Beyond confirming the diagnosis, what does the child's age most specifically raise concern for?
opts: A higher likelihood that this is simple idiopathic intussusception from lymphoid hyperplasia
A higher likelihood of an underlying pathologic lead point (PLP) that must be actively looked for
A lower likelihood of successful surgical treatment
No particular significance - age does not affect intussusception workup
exp: Idiopathic intussusception from Peyer's-patch lymphoid hyperplasia clusters under age 2; a 6-year-old is an atypical age and should trigger an active search for a pathologic lead point (Meckel diverticulum, lymphoma, polyp, duplication cyst, HSP) rather than a default 'idiopathic' label. Age is diagnostic information here, not demographic detail.

subject: Paediatrics
q: Classic idiopathic ileocolic intussusception, driven by Peyer's-patch lymphoid hyperplasia (often post-viral), shows its peak incidence in which age group?
exp: Idiopathic ileocolic intussusception peaks at 5-9 months, with roughly 80-90% of all cases occurring before age 2. Presentation outside this window, as in a 6-year-old, should raise rather than lower suspicion for an underlying pathologic lead point.

subject: Paediatrics
q: Which statement about pathologic lead points (PLP) in childhood intussusception is most accurate?
opts: Meckel diverticulum is the classic overall commonest PLP; in children specifically beyond 6 years, lymphoma (Burkitt/non-Hodgkin, ileocecal) is an important and often-cited cause
PLPs are exclusively seen in infants under 1 year
Appendiceal disease is the single most common PLP at every age
A PLP, once present, can never be reduced non-operatively regardless of type
exp: Meckel diverticulum is the classic overall commonest pathologic lead point in childhood intussusception. In children specifically beyond about 6 years, lymphoma (usually Burkitt or non-Hodgkin, ileocecal in location) becomes an important and frequently-tested cause - this age/lead-point pairing is a favourite exam distractor-buster, since most students default to 'idiopathic' regardless of age.

subject: Paediatrics
q: A 6-year-old with confirmed intussusception has no history of red, jelly-like stools and no palpable abdominal mass on the referral note. How should the absence of the classic 'currant-jelly stool plus sausage mass' triad be interpreted?
opts: All three triad features together are seen only in a minority even of infants; their absence does not argue against the diagnosis, especially early or in an older child
It means the diagnosis must be revised to simple gastroenteritis
It confirms an ileo-ileal rather than ileocolic type
exp: The full triad - colicky pain, currant-jelly stool, and a palpable sausage-shaped mass - is seen together in only a minority even of infants, and less often in older children or early presentations. Its absence does not argue against the diagnosis once imaging is positive; don't wait for the complete textbook triad before considering intussusception.

subject: Paediatrics
q: Which ultrasound finding, seen on transverse section, is considered essentially diagnostic of intussusception?
exp: The target or doughnut sign on transverse ultrasound (alternating hyper- and hypoechoic rings from the telescoped bowel wall), with the pseudokidney/sandwich sign on longitudinal section, is essentially diagnostic of intussusception. Ultrasound is first-line, and further cross-sectional imaging is not routinely required once it is positive.

subject: Paediatrics
q: A child is found to have an ileo-ileal (small-bowel-only) intussusception on ultrasound, rather than the usual ileocolic type. Which of the following is most true of this variant?
opts: It is more amenable to air enema reduction than ileocolic disease
It should raise suspicion for HSP (Henoch-Schonlein purpura)-related submucosal haematoma as the lead point, and is less often reducible by enema
It is the classic presentation of idiopathic post-viral intussusception
It requires no further workup once identified
exp: Ileo-ileal intussusception should raise suspicion for a pathologic lead point such as an HSP-related submucosal haematoma (from IgA vasculitis causing bowel-wall bleeding), and is less often reducible by air/hydrostatic enema than the far more common ileocolic type, which is designed to push the mass back around the ileocecal valve.

subject: Paediatrics
q: In a haemodynamically stable child with intussusception and no peritonism, perforation, or shock, what is the preferred first-line treatment?
opts: Immediate laparotomy in all cases regardless of stability
Non-operative reduction, with pneumatic (air) enema generally preferred over hydrostatic for higher success and lower perforation risk
Observation alone with no active intervention
exp: Non-operative reduction is first-line in a stable child without peritonism, perforation, or shock, with pneumatic (air) enema generally preferred over hydrostatic (saline/contrast) enema for a higher reduction success rate and a lower risk of perforation. Surgery is reserved for failure or specific red flags such as peritonitis or a suspected lead point.

subject: Paediatrics
q: Which of the following would push management toward surgery rather than a further attempt at enema reduction?
opts: A first episode of ileocolic intussusception in an 8-month-old with a normal abdominal exam
Peritonitis, perforation, shock, failed enema reduction, ileo-ileal type, or a suspected/visualised pathologic lead point
A CRP that is completely normal
exp: Peritonitis, perforation, shock, a failed enema reduction attempt, ileo-ileal type, recurrent intussusception, or a suspected/visualised pathologic lead point all favour surgical management. A young infant with a first episode and a reassuring exam is the opposite scenario - it favours a non-operative attempt first.

subject: Paediatrics
q: In a 6-year-old with confirmed intussusception, counts are normal but CRP is mildly elevated at 16. What is the best interpretation of this finding?
opts: It rules out the diagnosis, since infection markers should be markedly elevated
It is diagnostic of established bowel perforation
A normal count does not exclude evolving bowel-wall compromise; a rising inflammatory marker should be read as a caution sign supporting urgent rather than elective referral, even with stable vitals
It has no clinical relevance and can be disregarded
exp: A normal white cell count does not exclude early bowel-wall compromise or ischemia. A mildly rising inflammatory marker like CRP, in the setting of confirmed intussusception, should be read as a caution sign for evolving bowel-wall injury and supports urgent rather than elective referral, even when vitals remain stable.

subject: Paediatrics
q: Even after a school-age child's intussusception is successfully reduced non-operatively, what is the recommended next step given this age group?
opts: Discharge immediately with no further workup, since successful reduction confirms an idiopathic cause
Actively search for a pathologic lead point (re-imaging, lower threshold for laparoscopy/colonoscopy) before closing the workup, since occult lymphoma or Meckel's can otherwise be missed
No follow-up is needed since recurrence risk is zero after reduction
exp: Because pathologic lead point prevalence rises steeply with age, a school-age child who reduces successfully still needs active surveillance for a lead point - re-imaging and a lower threshold for laparoscopy/colonoscopy - before the workup is closed. Skipping this step risks discharging an occult lymphoma or Meckel diverticulum as 'resolved idiopathic intussusception.'

subject: Paediatrics
q: A term neonate born after an antenatal diagnosis of isolated fetal microcephaly (normal abdominal circumference and femur length throughout pregnancy) has a birth head circumference of 31 cm, below the 3rd centile. What is the most appropriate approach to monitoring this infant's growth after discharge?
opts: Serial head circumference plotting on a standard growth chart at every visit, watching for further deceleration in velocity
A single head circumference measurement at 6 months is sufficient to rule out ongoing pathology
Reassure the family that catch-up growth of head circumference always occurs by 3 months in isolated cases
Chart only weight and length; head circumference tracking is not needed once feet-first growth normalizes
exp: In infants with antenatally suspected isolated microcephaly, postnatal management hinges on serial (not single-point) head circumference measurement plotted on the IAP/WHO growth chart at every well-baby visit -- a static low percentile may simply reflect a small-but-normal head, but a falling growth velocity (crossing centiles downward) signals ongoing pathology and warrants neurodevelopmental referral; a one-off measurement cannot capture this trend.

subject: Paediatrics
q: A term neonate fails to pass meconium in the first 48 hours of life, followed by progressive abdominal distension and bilious vomiting. Digital rectal examination is followed by explosive expulsion of gas and stool. Which investigation is most likely to confirm the diagnosis?
opts: Contrast (barium) enema showing a transition zone
Rectal suction biopsy showing absence of ganglion cells
Anorectal manometry showing an absent rectoanal inhibitory reflex
exp: Rectal suction biopsy demonstrating absence of ganglion cells in the myenteric and submucosal plexuses, with hypertrophied nerve trunks, is the gold standard for confirming Hirschsprung disease. Contrast enema and anorectal manometry are useful screening tools but are not diagnostic on their own.

subject: Paediatrics
q: A 7-month-old boy presents with episodic colicky abdominal pain, drawing up of the legs, and passage of red currant-jelly stools. Abdominal examination reveals a sausage-shaped mass in the right hypochondrium. What is the best initial investigation, which can also be therapeutic in this condition?
exp: In a hemodynamically stable infant with intussusception and no signs of perforation or peritonitis, ultrasound confirms the target/doughnut sign and pneumatic (air) or hydrostatic enema reduction under image guidance is both diagnostic and first-line therapeutic, avoiding surgery in most cases.

subject: Paediatrics
q: A 5-week-old exclusively breastfed male infant has had progressively worsening non-bilious projectile vomiting after every feed for the past one week, remains hungry immediately after vomiting, and on examination has visible peristalsis and a palpable olive-shaped mass in the right upper quadrant. Which acid-base and electrolyte abnormality is most likely on venous blood gas?
opts: Respiratory alkalosis with compensatory metabolic acidosis
exp: In hypertrophic pyloric stenosis, repeated vomiting of gastric HCl and potassium-rich fluid produces the classic hypochloremic, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis with paradoxical aciduria (the kidney preferentially reabsorbs H+ over K+ to conserve volume). The clinical triad of non-bilious projectile vomiting, a hungry infant, and an olive-shaped RUQ mass should trigger this electrolyte prediction even before imaging.

subject: Paediatrics
q: A 16-month-old listed for elective circumcision is found on pre-op workup to have Hb 7.4 g/dL, microcytic hypochromic RBCs, low serum iron, low ferritin and high TIBC. Diet history: over 700 mL of cow's milk daily with poor solid intake. Most appropriate immediate management?
opts: Proceed with surgery under GA with blood cross-matched
Defer surgery; start oral elemental iron and reduce cow's milk intake
Give one unit of packed red cells, then proceed with surgery
Start empirical antihelminthic therapy and reassess in 1 week
exp: Elective surgery is deferred for significant anemia (Hb 7.4); correct with iron and dietary change — not transfusion for an asymptomatic, non-urgent case.

subject: Paediatrics
q: Which single mechanism does NOT contribute to cow's-milk-associated iron deficiency anemia in toddlers?
opts: Low iron content and poor bioavailability of cow's milk
Displacement of iron-rich weaning foods from the diet
Occult GI blood loss from milk-protein enteropathy
Direct destruction of red cells by lactose in cow's milk
exp: Lactose does not cause haemolysis; the real mechanisms are poor bioavailability, dietary displacement and occult GI blood loss.

subject: Paediatrics
q: A child's CBC shows Hb 8.2 g/dL, MCV 58 fl, RBC count 5.2 million/µL. What does the Mentzer index suggest, and what next?
opts: Index >13 — iron deficiency; start iron and recheck
Index <13 — thalassemia trait; iron studies and HbA2 electrophoresis indicated
Index not calculable from these values
Index <13 — confirms iron deficiency; start empirical iron
exp: Mentzer index = 58/5.2 = 11.2 (<13), pointing to thalassemia trait — needs iron studies + HbA2, not empirical iron.

subject: Paediatrics
q: Per current guidance, cow's milk should not be a primary drink before what age, and what is the recommended maximum daily volume after 1 year?
opts: 12 months; unlimited if iron-rich foods are also given
exp: AAP/IAP: no cow's milk before 12 months; 16–24 oz/day (2–3 cups) thereafter.

subject: Paediatrics
q: Correct elemental iron dose and minimum duration of therapy for a toddler with confirmed IDA?
opts: 3–6 mg/kg/day, continued ~3 months after Hb normalizes
IV iron sucrose regardless of severity
exp: 3–6 mg/kg/day elemental iron, continued ~3 months past Hb normalization to rebuild stores.

subject: Paediatrics
q: A peripheral smear from an anemic toddler shows microcytic hypochromic cells with marked anisopoikilocytosis and occasional pencil-shaped cells. Most consistent with:
exp: Microcytic, hypochromic cells with anisopoikilocytosis and pencil cells is the classic IDA smear.

subject: Paediatrics
q: In a toddler with a background febrile illness, serum ferritin is reported as 'normal' despite strong suspicion of iron deficiency. Most likely explanation?
opts: Ferritin is unaffected by inflammation, so iron deficiency is excluded
Ferritin is an acute-phase reactant and can be falsely normal/elevated during inflammation
The child cannot have iron deficiency if ferritin is normal, regardless of context
Ferritin is only useful in adults, not children
exp: Ferritin rises with inflammation/infection and can mask true iron deficiency; interpret cautiously in sick children.

subject: Paediatrics
q: After starting oral iron for confirmed IDA, the earliest objective marker of an adequate response, and its timing, is:
exp: Reticulocytosis peaking at day 5–7 is the earliest reliable sign of response; Hb rise and symptom resolution lag.

subject: Paediatrics
q: Which lab finding best distinguishes iron deficiency anemia from anemia of chronic disease, given both can show low serum iron?
opts: TIBC — elevated in IDA, reduced or normal in anemia of chronic disease
MCV alone, as both are always microcytic
exp: TIBC is the discriminator: high in IDA, low/normal in anemia of chronic disease.

subject: Paediatrics
q: A 14-month-old with chronic excessive cow's milk intake and undiagnosed IDA is most specifically at risk of which long-term complication?
exp: Developmental delay and pica are the classically tested long-term complications of untreated toddler IDA.

subject: Paediatrics
q: A baby born at 28 weeks gestation with a birth weight of 1100 g is now 4 weeks old, clinically stable, and off supplemental oxygen. As per the AAP/AAO joint retinopathy-of-prematurity screening statement, when should the first fundus examination be performed?
opts: Within the first week of life, regardless of gestation
At 6 weeks of postnatal age, regardless of gestational age
At 4 weeks postnatal age, or 31 weeks postmenstrual age, whichever is later
why: Too early — retinal vascularization has not reached a stage where ROP is detectable
A fixed rule that ignores postmenstrual age, the more physiologically relevant marker in very preterm infants
Far too late for a baby this premature; sight-threatening ROP can develop well before then
Correct — the standard AAP/NNF-anchored screening timing
exp: ROP screening timing is anchored to postmenstrual age, not chronological age alone: the first exam is done at 4 weeks postnatal age or 31 weeks postmenstrual age, whichever is later, in infants meeting standard risk criteria — because retinal vessels have not reached the watershed zone where clinically significant ROP develops until then.

subject: Paediatrics
q: A 9-year-old boy with fever for 18 days, currently on empirical antibiotics, develops sudden severe abdominal pain, distension, and guarding. An erect abdominal X-ray shows free air under the diaphragm. Which complication has most likely occurred, and in which week of illness does it classically arise?
opts: Ileal (Peyer's patch) perforation, classically occurring in the third week of enteric fever
why: Not the classic enteric-fever complication, and this timing is wrong for it
Cholecystitis can occur in typhoid but is not suggested by pneumoperitoneum
Not a recognized typhoid complication at this timing
Correct — classic third-week complication of enteric fever
exp: Intestinal perforation, usually of the terminal ileum over necrotic Peyer's patches, is the most feared complication of enteric fever and classically occurs in the third week of illness; it is a surgical emergency, and mortality rises sharply with delayed recognition, so free air on X-ray in a prolonged-fever child demands urgent surgical referral.

subject: Paediatrics
q: A 6-year-old boy snores loudly every night, has witnessed pauses in breathing during sleep, and shows daytime hyperactivity with declining school performance. Examination reveals grade 3 tonsillar hypertrophy. What is the gold-standard investigation to confirm the suspected diagnosis?
why: Can assess adenoid size but does not confirm or quantify sleep-disordered breathing
Correct — the gold-standard test to diagnose and grade pediatric OSA
Assesses airway obstruction/asthma, not sleep apnea
Not indicated for routine OSA diagnosis and carries unnecessary radiation
exp: Pediatric obstructive sleep apnea from adenotonsillar hypertrophy presents with snoring, witnessed apneas, and daytime behavioural/cognitive symptoms; overnight polysomnography remains the gold-standard confirmatory test, and adenotonsillectomy is first-line treatment once OSA is confirmed in a child with significant tonsillar hypertrophy.

subject: Paediatrics
q: A 2-week-old, exclusively breastfed neonate presents with jaundice, vomiting, poor feeding, and hepatomegaly, and blood culture grows E. coli. Urine testing is positive for reducing substances but negative for glucose on a glucose-oxidase dipstick. Which enzyme deficiency is most likely responsible?
why: Correct — classic galactosemia's textbook neonatal presentation, including the E. coli sepsis predisposition
Hereditary fructose intolerance presents only after fructose/sucrose exposure, not with exclusive breastfeeding
Von Gierke disease presents with fasting hypoglycemia and lactic acidosis, not this picture
PKU is typically asymptomatic in the neonatal period and does not cause reducing substances in urine
exp: Classic galactosemia (GALT deficiency) should be suspected in a jaundiced, vomiting neonate with hepatomegaly and E. coli sepsis after milk feeds begin; a urine reducing-substance test that is positive but glucose-oxidase-negative points to a non-glucose sugar (galactose) and mandates immediate lactose/galactose exclusion from feeds pending confirmatory testing.

subject: Paediatrics
q: An 8-year-old boy with asthma and allergic rhinitis presents with intermittent dysphagia to solid foods and an episode of food-bolus impaction requiring endoscopic removal. Upper GI endoscopy shows longitudinal furrows and white exudates in the esophagus. Esophageal biopsy is most likely to show which finding?
opts: Absent ganglion cells in the submucosal plexus
Dense eosinophilic infiltrate (greater than 15 eosinophils per high-power field) confined to the esophagus
Helicobacter pylori organisms with chronic active gastritis
why: Villous atrophy is the celiac disease finding, in the duodenum
Absent ganglion cells describes Hirschsprung disease, a colonic/rectal condition
Correct — the atopic history plus endoscopic picture is classic for eosinophilic esophagitis
H. pylori gastritis causes epigastric pain/peptic disease, not this endoscopic picture
exp: Eosinophilic esophagitis should be suspected in an atopic child (asthma/rhinitis/eczema/food allergy) with dysphagia or food impaction; endoscopy classically shows furrows, rings, or white exudates, and diagnosis requires biopsy showing more than 15 eosinophils per high-power field, distinguishing it from GERD.

subject: Paediatrics
q: A 10-year-old girl has height persistently below the 3rd percentile for age, a webbed neck, widely spaced nipples, and cubitus valgus, with subnormal growth velocity since early childhood. Which investigation is most important to confirm the underlying diagnosis?
opts: Karyotype analysis (looking for 45,X or a mosaic pattern)
Bone age X-ray of the left wrist
why: Correct — karyotype confirms the classic Turner syndrome picture described
Diagnoses isolated growth hormone deficiency, not this syndromic picture
Helps assess growth potential/puberty timing but does not confirm the chromosomal diagnosis
Should be checked as part of the short-stature work-up but will not confirm this specific syndrome
exp: Any girl with unexplained short stature should have a karyotype checked, even without every classic Turner stigma present, because the phenotype can be subtle; confirmed Turner syndrome (45,X or mosaicism) needs echocardiography, renal ultrasound, and audiology screening in addition to growth hormone therapy and later pubertal induction.

subject: Paediatrics
q: An 18-month-old boy has failure to thrive, polyuria, and rachitic wrist widening. Labs show normoglycemic glucosuria, generalized aminoaciduria, and hypophosphatemia with metabolic acidosis. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
why: Distal RTA causes hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis with urine pH above 5.5, but not glucosuria, aminoaciduria or phosphaturia.
Bartter syndrome causes hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis and polyuria from a thick-ascending-limb defect, not glucosuria or aminoaciduria.
Correct — proximal tubule dysfunction spills glucose, amino acids, phosphate and bicarbonate together, producing rickets and failure to thrive; cystinosis is the classic paediatric cause.
Nephrogenic diabetes insipidus causes polyuria/polydipsia from ADH resistance alone, with no glucosuria, aminoaciduria or phosphaturia.
exp: Fanconi syndrome (generalized proximal tubulopathy) causes normoglycemic glucosuria, aminoaciduria, phosphaturia, and proximal RTA together, producing rickets and failure to thrive. Cystinosis is the most common inherited cause in children and needs cystine-depleting therapy (cysteamine) to prevent progression to ESRD.
